But what is it that we sinned in and with Adam? That Adam's sin is imputed to us? So D. Garissolius takes it in chapter 8, section 21. For how, he says, could those who existed many ages later have already sinned before in another, unless because he performed that act which is so reckoned of posterity as if they themselves had committed it? And he adds that the theologians, when they teach that we have satisfied in Christ, mean nothing else than that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us. This interpretation of his fits what he often presses: that Adam's sin is ours only by imputation. From this it follows that we did not sin in and with Adam except imputatively. But then the reasoning of the most learned theologians would turn out trifling. For they would prove the same by the same — the imputation of Adam's sin by the imputation of Adam's sin — which trifling, especially in so grave a Decree, it is wrong to assign to them. What, then, does that phrase mean? It can be understood from a like case. For if someone said that we were in and with Adam, the sense would be not that Adam's being is imputed to us, but that Adam's being was communicated to us by natural propagation. So when we are said to have sinned in and with Adam, the sense is not that Adam's sin is imputed to us (for that would be, as I said, to import a trifling into the Decree of most excellent men), but that Adam's sin was communicated to us by natural propagation. From which it follows that it is justly imputed to us — but by mediate or consequent imputation, which Placeus constantly acknowledges and holds.

source_text:
Ut sit finis, illi ipsi, qui Decretum Synodi Nationalis fecerunt, sententiae meae allipulantur, suoque testimonio Placeum a condemnatione liberant, in primis Clarissimus et piissimus vir D. Drelincourtius, fidelissimus Ecclesiae Parisiensis Pastor. Cum enim hucusque in hoc scripto progressus essem, id, antequam prodiret in lucem, cum quibusdam amicis suis viris doctissimis et prudentissimis communicatum Placeus voluit, praecipue vero cum dicto D. Drelincourtio, cuius in conficiendo illo Decreto plurimum valuisse auctoritatem non ignorabat. Is autem eo perlecto pro suo insigni candore et pacis Ecclesiae studio humanissimas scripsit ad Placeum literas Lutetia, An. 1653. die 10. Decemb., quas, cum bona eius venia, huc transcribere non gravabor: interest enim et veritatis, et pacis, et causae quam ago, ut in vulgus emanent. Erant autem Gallico sermone ita conceptae; in gratiam eorum qui Gallice nesciunt eas Latine vertit Placeus:

Domine et honorande Frater. Scriptum, quod mecum communicatum voluisti, singulari cum voluptate legi; quodque eo finitum id videam, unde Ecclesiis nostris perturbationem aliquam et divisionem metuebam, Deo ex toto corde gratias ago. Possum enim tibi, Domine, aliisque omnibus, si qui dubitant, confirmare, consilium ultimae Synodi Nationalis Carentonensis nullo modo fuisse te, tuamve quam proponis doctrinam condemnare. Id pro certo testari possum. Quippe cum dignus habitus fuerim, qui non modo celebri illi conventui interessem, sed etiam unus essem ex delegatis illis qui Decretum, de quo agitur, conscripserunt. Nunquam nobis in mentem venit eam imputationem peccati Adamici constabilire, quam tu antecedentem et immediatam appellas, sed eam duntaxat quam tu consequentem et mediatam vocas. Ego quidem ita perpetuo sensi et docui. Quocirca magno gaudio et consolatione afficior, quod videam de hoc momentosissimo dogmate te mecum idem sentire. Si tui apud eos iustificandi, qui haec aut non satis intelligunt aut adversus praeiudiciis laborant, sese mihi dederit occasio, confirmo tibi me causae tuae non defuturum. Interest gloriae Dei et publicae aedificationis ut haec veritas omnibus innotescat, nihil ut sit quod obstet, quominus quibus te ditavit Deus dotes insignes ubique fructum ferant. Ego te toto pectore complector, et sum, etc.

Quid potes amplius ad plenam Placei iustificationem, Lector pie, desiderare?
english: To make an end: those very men who made the Decree of the National Synod assent to my judgment, and by their testimony free Placeus from condemnation — above all the most distinguished and most pious man D. Drelincourt, most faithful pastor of the church of Paris. For when I had progressed this far in this writing, Placeus wished it, before it came into the light, to be shared with certain of his friends, most learned and most prudent men — and especially with the said D. Drelincourt, whose authority he was not unaware had weighed very much in drafting that Decree. And he, having read it through, for his outstanding candor and zeal for the church's peace wrote most kind letters to Placeus from Paris, in the year 1653, on the 10th of December, which, with his good leave, I will not be reluctant to copy here: for it concerns truth, and peace, and the cause I plead, that they go out among the people. They were framed in the French tongue; for the sake of those who do not know French Placeus turned them into Latin: Lord and honored Brother. The writing which you wished to be shared with me I read with singular pleasure; and that I see finished by it that from which I feared some disturbance and division in our churches, I give thanks to God from my whole heart. For I can confirm to you, Lord, and to all others if any doubt, that the counsel of the last National Synod of Charenton was in no way to condemn you, or the doctrine which you propose. That I can testify for certain. For I was counted worthy not only to be present in that famous assembly, but also to be one of those delegates who drafted the Decree of which we speak. It never entered our mind to establish that imputation of Adam's sin which you call antecedent and immediate, but only that which you call consequent and mediate. I for my part have always so thought and taught. So I am filled with great joy and consolation that I see you feel the same with me concerning this most momentous dogma. If occasion offers itself to me of justifying you before those who either do not sufficiently understand these things or labor under adverse prejudices, I confirm to you that I will not fail your cause. It concerns the glory of God and public edification that this truth become known to all, so that there be nothing to hinder the excellent gifts with which God has enriched you from bearing fruit everywhere. I embrace you with my whole heart, and am, etc. What more can you desire, pious reader, for Placeus's full justification?

source_text:
CAPUT V. Distributio dicendorum.

Reconciliato cum Synodo Placeo, nihil superest, nisi ut stantes utrinque argumentorum acies, alteram pro imputatione, alteram contra imputationem primi Adae peccati, conciliemus inter se, ut positis odiis, sublata dissensione, coniunctis viribus ad Decretum Synodi tuendum et confirmandum quicquid habent roboris concorditer conferant. Id autem fiet, si demonstraverimus, neque argumenta, quae pro imputatione primae Adae inobedientiae afferuntur, quicquam valere ad probandam imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam, neque argumenta, quae contra peccati illius imputationem proferuntur, ullam vim habere adversus imputationem consequentem seu mediatam. Ubi enim patuerit, nec illa probare imputationem quam ista improbant, nec ista eam improbare quam illa probant, nonne manifestum evadet, in speciem tantum inter se argumenta illa pugnare, re autem vera conspirare amice ad imputationem mediatam, repudiata immediata, firmandam, Decretumque Synodi, ut a me expositum est, defendendum? Nisi hoc utrumque praestitero, species illa repugnantiae terrorem perpetuo incutiet, et bellum veluti intentabit, nec, intercedentibus praeiudiciis, nonnullisque fortasse perturbationibus, firmae pacis constabiliendae spes certa exorietur. In id igitur mihi totis viribus incumbendum est, ut utrumque illud demonstrem. Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum supplex rogo, ut mihi id facere indulgeat ita clare et efficaciter, ut omnis in posterum de hac re dubitandi dissentiendique ansa prorsus tollatur, omnesque virtute et unitate eiusdem Spiritus sancti in eandem sententiam conveniamus, in eaque constanter perseveremus. Amen.

Hoc autem ordine procedemus. Primum argumenta quae pro imputatione primi Adae peccati afferuntur, ad examen revocabimus, et planum faciemus, si quam peccati illius imputationem probant, eam nonnisi consequentem seu Mediatam esse. Deinde argumenta quae contra imputationem primi illius peccati militare videntur, similiter ponderabimus, nullamque vim habere ostendemus, nisi adversus imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam. Ita hae duae erunt partes eorum quae nobis dicenda restant.
english: Chapter Five. Distribution of what is to be said.

Placeus having been reconciled with the Synod, nothing remains except that we reconcile with each other the lines of argument standing on either side — the one for imputation, the other against imputation of Adam's first sin — so that, hatreds laid down and dissension removed, with joined strength they may together contribute whatever force they have to defending and confirming the Synod's Decree. And that will happen if we demonstrate that neither the arguments brought forward for the imputation of Adam's first disobedience avail anything toward proving antecedent or immediate imputation, nor the arguments brought against the imputation of that sin have any force against consequent or mediate imputation. For when it has become plain that the former do not prove the imputation which the latter reject, and that the latter do not reject the imputation which the former prove, will it not become manifest that those arguments fight among themselves only in appearance, but in truth conspire amicably to establish mediate imputation, the immediate having been repudiated, and to defend the Synod's Decree as I have set it forth? Unless I accomplish both, that appearance of conflict will perpetually strike terror and will, as it were, threaten war; nor, with prejudices intervening and perhaps some disturbances, will a sure hope of establishing firm peace arise. Therefore I must throw my whole strength into demonstrating both. I ask our Lord Jesus Christ as a suppliant that he grant me to do it so clearly and effectually that every handle for doubting and dissenting about this matter afterward be utterly taken away, and that we all by the power and unity of the same Holy Spirit come into the same judgment and constantly persevere in it. Amen.

And we will proceed in this order. First we will call back to examination the arguments brought forward for the imputation of Adam's first sin, and we will make it plain that if they prove any imputation of that sin, it is only consequent or Mediate. Then we will likewise weigh the arguments that seem to fight against the imputation of that first sin, and we will show that they have no force except against antecedent or immediate imputation. So these will be the two parts of what remains for us to say.

source_text:
CAPUT VI. Non aliam imputationem primi Adae peccati, quam consequentem seu mediatam, Argumenta Clariss. D. Maresii probare.

Post ultimam Synodum Nationalem pro imputatione primi Adae peccati scripserunt libris typis excusis, quos quidem viderim, Clarissimi viri, Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Maresius, Ant. Garissolius, Carolus Daubuz, et Steph. Blancus, manuscriptis vero alii complures. Sed primus illorum celeberrimus Rivetus non auctoritate Scripturae, nec rationibus, sed corrasis undecunque potuit virorum doctorum testimoniis, etiam adhuc viventium, eorumque nonnullorum, quorum nomen nobis antea inauditum fuerat, pugnandum sibi censuit; itaque nunc quidem omittatur. Docet enim prius audiri eos qui testimonia Scripturae, et argumenta afferunt. Non enim quaerimus quid homines sentiant, sed quid nobis sentiendum sit, quid Deus nos sentire voluerit. Regula fidei nostrae est Dei verbum, non hominum opiniones. His ergo in ultimum locum rejectis, deprompta e Scripturis argumenta inspiciamus.
english: Chapter Six. That the arguments of the most distinguished D. Maresius prove no other imputation of Adam’s first sin than the consequent or mediate.

After the last National Synod, several most distinguished men wrote in print — at least among the books I have seen — for the imputation of Adam’s first sin: Andreas Rivetus, Samuel Maresius, Antoine Garissoles, Charles Daubuz, and Stephen Blanc. Many others wrote in manuscript. The first of them, the celebrated Rivetus, chose to fight neither by Scripture’s authority nor by reasons, but by testimonies of learned men scraped together from every quarter, including living writers whose names we had never even heard of before. For now, then, set him aside. Hear first those who bring Scripture’s testimonies and arguments. We are not asking what men think; we are asking what we ought to think, and what God has willed us to think. God’s word is the rule of our faith, not men’s opinions. Push those opinion-collectors to the rear, and let us examine the arguments drawn from the Scriptures.

source_text:
Prodiit Groningae apud Ioan. Nicolaum Anno Domini M. DC. XLVI. Theologiae Elenchticae nova Synopsis, sive Index controversiarum fidei ex sacris Scripturis a Iacobo Tirino Iesuita concinnatus, et Censura perpetua auctus, emendatus, refutatus, per Samuelem Maresium S. Theol. D. eiusdemque Facultatis Professorem ordinarium in Academia Provinciali Groningae et Omlandiae. In quo, Controversia xx. de statu primorum parentum et de peccato originali, Num. 4, occasione quorundam Tirini verborum, digreditur vir clarissimus in Controversiam istam de imputatione primae Adami inobedientiae, ac cum Socini, Curcellaei, aliorumque omnem imputationem illius peccati negantium, nec-non Decreti Synodi Nationalis Ecclesiarum Galliae, libellique a Cl. Riveto editi meminisset, subjecit: Nec solum οἱ ἐναντίοι illam imputationem impugnant, sed etiam (quae fuit occasio illius Decreti Synodici) Rev. doctissimus ac celeberrimus vir, meus quondam Commilito in studiis suavissimus D. Iosue Placeus Disput. Salmur. parte I. p. 206. et seqq. illam omnino rejicit praeter ius et fas, dum bene et orthodoxe studet propugnare haereditariam, quae omnibus inest, corruptionem: cum et illa debeat admitti, et haec sit agnoscenda, utpote quae pari passu ambulent; sic tamen ut ordine naturae, et insigni rationis traducem innatae corruptionis, primi peccati praecedat imputatio.

Ejus se Commilitonem in studiis non sine voluptate Placeus reminiscitur, veterisque amicitiae reliquias in elogiis illis agnoscit, quibus se minime dignum ab eo ornari videt: optasset tamen clarissimum virum adversus Iesuitam scribentem, hujus, si quam inter nos esse putat, controversiae non meminisse, nolletque se ab amico in eundem quasi fasciculum cum Curcellaeo, a quo vehementer dissentit, compactum esse. In posterum, uti spero, vir doctissimus Placeum neque condemnatum a Synodo Nationali fuisse, neque imputationem primi Adae peccati omnino rejicere, sibi affirmandum putabit. Non enim opinor, existimabit, Dei gloriam Ecclesiaeque aedificationem flagitare, ut pro condemnato ab omnibus habeatur. Quod autem ait, imputationem et corruptionem pari passu ambulare, si imputationem intelligeret consequentem, non me haberet repugnantem, sed cum antecedentem intelligere videatur, ei assentiri non possum. Illa enim imputatio nullo modo, nec Scriptura, nec ratione, Scripturae et rationi repugnans; haec vero corruptio multis Scripturae testimoniis, multis rationibus, ipsaque adeo experientia certissime probari potest.

Talia praefatus vir Clariss. subiungit haec pauca argumenta verbis brevissimis, quibus etiam brevissime respondebimus.
english: There came forth at Groningen from John Nicolas in the year of the Lord 1646 A New Synopsis of Elenctic Theology, or Index of the controversies of the faith from the Holy Scriptures compiled by Jacob Tirinus the Jesuit, and enlarged, emended, and refuted with a perpetual Censure, by Samuel Maresius, Doctor of Sacred Theology and ordinary Professor of the same Faculty in the Provincial Academy of Groningen and Omland. In which, Controversy 20, on the state of the first parents and on original sin, number 4, on occasion of certain words of Tirinus, the most distinguished man digresses into that Controversy on the imputation of Adam's first disobedience, and when he had made mention of Socinus, Curcellaeus, and others who deny all imputation of that sin, and also of the Decree of the National Synod of the Churches of France, and of the booklet edited by the distinguished Rivetus, he added: Not only do the opponents attack that imputation, but also (which was the occasion of that Synodical Decree) the Reverend, most learned and most celebrated man, my former most sweet fellow-soldier in studies, D. Josué Placeus, Disputations of Saumur, part I, page 206 and following, entirely rejects it beyond right and law, while he studies well and orthodoxly to defend the hereditary corruption which is in all: since both that ought to be admitted, and this is to be acknowledged, as walking with equal step; yet so that by order of nature, and by the notable reason of the transplant of inborn corruption, the imputation of the first sin should precede.

That he was his fellow-soldier in studies Placeus remembers not without pleasure, and he recognizes the remains of old friendship in those praises with which he sees himself adorned by him though least worthy: yet he would have wished that the most distinguished man, writing against the Jesuit, had not mentioned this controversy, if he thinks there is any between us, and he would not want to be packed by a friend into the same bundle, as it were, with Curcellaeus, from whom he vehemently differs. Hereafter, as I hope, the most learned man will think he should affirm that Placeus was neither condemned by the National Synod, nor does he entirely reject the imputation of Adam's first sin. For I do not think he will judge that God's glory and the church's edification demand that he be held for condemned by all. But as to what he says, that imputation and corruption walk with equal step — if he understood consequent imputation, he would not have me resisting; but since he seems to understand antecedent, I cannot assent to him. For that imputation is in no way, neither by Scripture nor by reason, repugnant to Scripture and reason; but this corruption can most certainly be proved by many testimonies of Scripture, by many reasons, and even by experience itself.
Having prefaced such things, the most distinguished man subjoins these few arguments in very brief words, to which we shall also reply most briefly.

source_text:
I. Eam culpam censeri illis imputari, qui eius reatui et poenae subiaceant, est certissimum. Omnes autem Adami posteros subjici reatui et poenae culpae, quam Adam commisit, tota clamat Scriptura, ac praesertim Rom. v. 12. 1. Cor. xv. 21. 22. Distinguo: clamat subiici subiectione, quae antecedat ordine naturae vitium haereditarium, Nego; subiectione, quae sequatur illud vitium, Concedo, testemque laudo ipsum D. Gariss. cap. 8. §. 3. p. 206.

II. Addit, Nec potest fieri, quin illis imputetur Adami transgressio, qui incurrunt poenam, mortem scilicet, illi transgressioni divinitus denunciatam. Nam ut bene dicuntur imputata Christo nostra peccata, quod poenam illis debitam sustinuerit, et recte nobis imputari censetur eius iustitia, quod eius meritum et praemium aeternum consequamur, ita Adami peccatum iis imputari dicendum, qui eius reatum et poenam sustinent. Respondeo, fieri quidem non posse, quin illis imputetur Adami transgressio, qui incurrunt poenam illi transgressioni denunciatam, sed manet integra quaestio, utrum eam immediate, ac ordine Naturae priusquam corrumpantur, incurrant, an vero tantum consequenter et mediante illa corruptione? Prius nego, nec probat D. Maresius, posterius affirmo. Ad Christum quod spectat, imputata sunt illi peccata nostra, non tanquam autori, sed tanquam innocentissimo peccatorum vadi: itaque propterea peccator dici non potuit. Nobis autem peccatum Adami imputatur, non tanquam illius vadibus, sed tanquam illius autoribus, ac vere peccatoribus. Itaque plurimum distant illae imputationes. Adde quod non sunt imputata peccata nostra Christo, imputatione antecedente, sed consequente tantum eius consensum, sine quo non potuissent ei imputari. Similiter discrimen magnum est inter iustitiae Christi et peccati Adamici imputationem. Illa enim ex gratia, hoc ex iustitia nobis imputatur: et tamen ipsa iustitiae imputatio non est immediata seu antecedens, sed consensum nostrum et fidem consequitur, absque quo nulla esset. Tantummodo est memorabilis differentia. Nam fides non est iustitia, nec meretur vitam aeternam, cum vitium haereditarium sit vere peccatum generi humano damnando sufficiens. Nimirum, ut dixi, imputatio iustitiae est ex gratia, peccati ex merito.
english: I. That that fault is judged to be imputed to those who are subject to its guilt and penalty is most certain. But that all Adam's posterity are subjected to the guilt and penalty of the fault which Adam committed, all Scripture cries out, and especially Romans 5:12, 1 Corinthians 15:21–22. I distinguish: it cries that they are subjected by a subjection which precedes hereditary vice by order of nature — I deny; by a subjection which follows that vice — I grant, and I praise as witness D. Garissoles himself, chapter 8, section 3, page 206.

II. He adds, Nor can it happen that Adam's transgression is not imputed to those who incur the penalty, namely death, divinely denounced upon that transgression. For as our sins are well said to be imputed to Christ, because he sustained the penalty due to them, and his righteousness is rightly judged to be imputed to us, because we obtain his merit and eternal reward, so Adam's sin is to be said to be imputed to those who sustain its guilt and penalty. I answer: it indeed cannot happen that Adam's transgression is not imputed to those who incur the penalty denounced upon that transgression, but the question remains entire, whether they incur it immediately, and by order of Nature before they are corrupted, or only consequently and through that corruption? The former I deny, and D. Maresius does not prove it; the latter I affirm. As to what concerns Christ, our sins were imputed to him, not as to an author, but as to the most innocent surety of sinners: and therefore he could not be called a sinner. But to us Adam's sin is imputed, not as to his sureties, but as to his authors, and truly sinners. And so those imputations stand far apart. Add that our sins were not imputed to Christ by antecedent imputation, but only by one consequent upon his consent, without which they could not have been imputed to him. Likewise there is a great difference between the imputation of Christ's righteousness and that of Adam's sin. For the former is imputed to us from grace, the latter from justice: and yet the imputation of righteousness itself is not immediate or antecedent, but follows our consent and faith, without which it would be none. There is only a memorable difference. For faith is not righteousness, nor does it merit eternal life, since hereditary vice is truly a sin sufficient for damning the human race. Namely, as I said, the imputation of righteousness is from grace, of sin from desert.

source_text:
III. Atque haec imputatio, inquit, non nititur solo Dei iure in creaturas, ac Dominio absoluto (ut quidam volunt) sed eius iustitia aequissima, ac valde iusto iudicio. Fateor, si imputatio intelligitur Mediata; Immediata enim (ut suo loco, Deo dante, manifestum faciam) cum divina iustitia non parum pugnat. Pergit, Nam saepe etiam hoc fit in foro humano absque ulla iniquitatis specie, sed iustissime, ut unius culpa peccatum et vitium universam communitatem aut posteritatem quoad poenae extensionem implicet, quod dum fit illa culpa toti vel communitati vel posteritati imputatur. Primum hoc in Lege sua damnat Deus disertis verbis Deut. 24. 16. etiam cum de crimine laesae Maiestatis agitur 2. Reg. 14. 6. vetatque ne tale quid de ipsius iustitia dicatur Ezech. 18. et Ierem. 31. 29. 30. Deinde, si unius culpa universam communitatem implicat, id fit, quia supponitur universa communitas in eam culpam consensisse: alioquin id iuste fieri nequit. Saepe, addit vir Clariss. evenit, ut quicquid delirent Reges, plectantur Achivi, nimirum illi non minus quam sui Reges delirabant.

Atque Procurator aut Mandatarius peccat iis peccat, quorum nomina sustinet. Nempe quia hi consenserant ut is eorum esset ea in re Procurator aut Mandatarius. Sequitur ergo imputatio, si quae est, eorum consensum, non antecedit. Quis autem nostrum, tanto antequam esset, suum unquam Procuratorem aut Mandatarium constituit Adamum? Multis in locis obtinet, ut si Vassallus infidelis fuerit suo Domino, peccet non solum sibi, sed suis posteris, qui sic feudo excidunt, alias ad se perventuro. Eatenus certe posteris peccat, quia feudum quod amisit, cum amplius non habeat, tradere liberis suis non potest. Id quod etiam evenit Adamo, qui, cum iustitiam originalem amisisset, eam in posteros propagare non potuit: quis enim dare possit id quod non habet? Nec tamen sequitur propterea infidelitatem posteris imputari. Nam si feudum vendidisset, aut potentioris vel vi, vel fraude amisisset, eo pariter, absque ullius culpae imputatione, privarentur posteri. Est apud Macedonas, addit vir doctus, crimen maiestatis ab aliquo commissum in universam eius cognationem vindicatum. Quid? An hominum crudelitatem ab ipsa Dei Lege damnatam putat vir clariss. Deum imitari? aut ex hominum iniustitia, quid Dei iustitiam deceat, debere colligi? Aliam ei mentem et opto, et esse puto.

Sequuntur in eius libro, Et quamvis maior sit mansuetudo Legum quae obtinent inter Christianos, saepe tamen evenit, ut laesae Maiestatis aliudve gravius crimen sic imputetur liberis et posteris eius qui illud commiserit, ut bonis suis in fiscum redactis, etiam nobilitatis gradu excidant. Nempe liberi opum et nobilitatis patris sunt heredes, si quas habet; si vero nullas habuit, aut habuit quidem, sed aut sua, aut nulla culpa amisit, qui earum possent esse heredes? Hoc vero quid ad imputationem antecedentem primae hominis inobedientiae probandam facere potest? Pestem contrahit aliquis saepenumero non soli sibi, sed domesticis etiam et vicinis suis. Num ulla sit eis propterea illius viri vel actionis, aut passionis, qua pestem contraxit, vel pestis ipsius imputatio?

Praeclare Chamierus Panstr. tom. 3. lib. 1. de hom. corrupto. cap. 8. §. 10. Atqui totam naturam (peccatum Adami) laesit, inquit Salmero: itaque factum est commune omnium. Nego consequentiam. Laesio ipsa facta est communis, at non causa laesionis. Sic si domus una conflagret, ut saepe fit, ob segnitiem Domini, indeque vicinae domus: erit quidem incendium commune: at segnities tota illius Domini, non reliquorum: non est enim segnities ipsa incendium, sed tantum causa incendii, quod ad reliquos pervenit. Sic qui miles excubias agit negligenter, nocet ille quidem toti exercitui: sed non fuit tamen totus exercitus segnis. Sic Neronis crudelitas Romanis nocuit: nec Romani tamen crudeles. Sexcenta sunt huiusmodi.
english: III. And this imputation, he says, does not rest on God's right over creatures alone, and on absolute Dominion (as some will have it), but on his most equal justice, and most just judgment. I grant it, if Mediate imputation is understood; for Immediate (as I shall make plain in its place, God granting) fights not a little with divine justice. He continues: For often this also happens in a human court without any appearance of iniquity, but most justly, that by one person's fault sin and vice implicate a whole community or posterity as to the extension of the penalty, which, while it happens, that fault is imputed to the whole community or posterity. First, God condemns this in his Law in express words, Deuteronomy 24:16, even when the crime of injured Majesty is in view, 2 Kings 14:6, and forbids that any such thing be said of his own justice, Ezekiel 18, and Jeremiah 31:29–30. Next, if one person's fault implicates a whole community, that happens because the whole community is supposed to have consented to that fault: otherwise it cannot justly be done. Often, the most distinguished man adds, it happens that whatever Kings rave, the Achaeans are punished — plainly those were raving no less than their Kings.

And a Procurator or Mandatory sins with a sin that belongs to those whose names he bears. Namely because these had consented that he should be their Procurator or Mandatory in that matter. Therefore imputation, if there is any, follows their consent; it does not precede it. But which of us, so long before he existed, ever appointed Adam his Procurator or Mandatory? In many places it obtains that if a Vassal has been unfaithful to his Lord, he sins not only for himself but for his posterity, who thus fall from the fief otherwise about to come to them. To that extent certainly he sins for his posterity, because the fief which he lost, since he no longer has it, he cannot hand over to his children. Which also happened to Adam, who, when he had lost original righteousness, could not propagate it into posterity: for who can give what he does not have? And yet it does not follow on that account that unfaithfulness is imputed to the posterity. For if he had sold the fief, or lost it by a stronger man's force or fraud, the posterity would likewise be deprived of it without any imputation of fault. Among the Macedonians, the learned man adds, the crime of majesty committed by someone was avenged upon his whole kinship. What then? Does the most distinguished man think God imitates men's cruelty condemned by God's own Law? Or that from men's injustice one ought to gather what befits God's justice? I both wish him another mind, and think he has one.

There follow in his book: And although the gentleness of the Laws which obtain among Christians is greater, yet it often happens that injured Majesty or another graver crime is so imputed to the children and posterity of him who committed it, that when their goods have been turned into the treasury they even fall from the grade of nobility. Namely children are heirs of the father's wealth and nobility, if he has any; but if he had none, or had them indeed but lost them either by his own fault or by none, who could be heirs of them? But what can this do toward proving the antecedent imputation of the first man's disobedience? Someone contracts a plague often not for himself alone but also for his household and neighbors. Is there therefore for them any imputation of that man's action or passion by which he contracted the plague, or of the plague itself?

Excellently Chamier, Panstratia, volume 3, book 1, on corrupt man, chapter 8, section 10: But he wounded the whole nature (Adam's sin), says Salmeron: therefore it was made common to all. I deny the consequence. The wounding itself was made common, but not the cause of the wounding. So if one house burns, as often happens, because of the Master's sloth, and thence neighboring houses: the fire will indeed be common; but the sloth is wholly that Master's, not the rest's: for sloth is not itself the fire, but only the cause of the fire which reaches the rest. So the soldier who keeps watch negligently harms the whole army: yet the whole army was not lazy. So Nero's cruelty harmed the Romans: and yet the Romans were not cruel. There are hundreds of this kind.

source_text:
IV. Superioribus alia quaedam Cl. Maresius adiungit argumenta. Ecquis vero, inquit, neget quod nos peccavimus, nobis merito iureque imputari? Iam autem nostrum esse quoque illud peccatum, clare docet Apostolus, qui omnes in Adamo peccasse asserit. Rom. 5. 12. Omnino quod nos peccavimus, nobis merito imputatur. Sed illud peccare nostrum prius est, saltem ordine naturae, ipsa illius imputatione. Praescinde ergo cogitatione imputationem, nosque si potes, demonstra peccasse ipsum primum actuale peccatum primi hominis. Qui antecedentem imputationem tenent, aiunt peccatum illud nostrum non esse nisi per imputationem. Si nostrum non est nisi imputatione, nostrum est quia nobis imputatur, non contra nobis imputatur quia nostrum est. Ad locum Apostoli quod attinet, nec verbo peccavimus primum actuale Adae peccatum significatur, nec Apostolus nobis videtur dicere in quo sed eo quod potius, nec si vertas in quo propterea elici ulla poterit imputatio, nisi forte consequens seu mediata, ut suo loco, Deo dante, demonstraturus sum.

V. Addit, Si enim in Abrahae lumbis decimatus est Levi, Heb. vii. 9. quanto magis in lumbis Adami nos omnes peccasse censebimur, utpote qui in illo essemus ut rami in radice, massa in primitiis, membra in capite, Rom. xi. 16. 1. Cor. xv. 22. Si quis similiter argumentaretur: Si in Abrahae lumbis decimatus est Levi, quanto magis in lumbis Sethi, vel Enoschi, vel alterius alicuius Patriarcharum qui ante diluvium vixerunt, nos omnes peccavimus? Probaretne consequentiam vir doctus? aut quid posset respondere, quod ei reponi similiter non possit? Nulla igitur est consequentia. Qua enim arte inde elicietur imputatio primi peccati actualis potius quam sequentium, et Adami potius quam Sethi aut Noachi, et antecedens potius quam consequens? Sed, ut liberaliter agam, fateor nos in lumbis Adami peccasse: num inde sequitur, nobis eius primum actuale peccatum imputari imputatione quae corruptionem haereditariam antecedat? sequitur contrarium potius. Peccavimus enim in Adamo, quia in eo fuimus. Fuimus autem in eo ut rami in radice. Ita autem sunt rami in radice, ut nihil radicis ramis imputetur proprie, sed trahant rami a radice naturam suam et succum vitalem, qualis est in radice, bonum vel malum. Sic nos ab Adamo corrupto naturam corruptam traximus. Ceterum nec massa in primitiis proprie fuit, sed in massa primitiae, nec alia membra in capite. Itaque hae comparationes ab eo quod agimus alienae videntur, nec ullam imputationem inducunt, nedum immediatam aut antecedentem.
english: IV. To the former the distinguished Maresius joins certain other arguments. And who indeed, he says, would deny that what we have sinned is deservedly and rightly imputed to us? But that that sin is ours also, the Apostle clearly teaches, who asserts that all have sinned in Adam. Romans 5:12. Wholly, what we have sinned is deservedly imputed to us. But that sinning of ours is prior, at least by order of nature, to the imputation itself. Therefore cut away imputation by thought, and show us, if you can, that we have sinned the very first actual sin of the first man. Those who hold antecedent imputation say that that sin is not ours except by imputation. If it is not ours except by imputation, it is ours because it is imputed to us, not on the contrary imputed to us because it is ours. As to what touches the Apostle's place, neither by the word we have sinned is the first actual sin of Adam signified, nor does the Apostle seem to us to say in whom but rather in that, nor if you turn it in whom can any imputation therefore be elicited, unless perhaps consequent or mediate, as in its place, God granting, I am going to demonstrate.

V. He adds, For if in Abraham's loins Levi was tithed, Hebrews 7:9, how much more shall we all be judged to have sinned in Adam's loins, inasmuch as we were in him as branches in a root, a mass in firstfruits, members in a head, Romans 11:16, 1 Corinthians 15:22. If anyone should argue similarly: If in Abraham's loins Levi was tithed, how much more in the loins of Seth, or of Enosh, or of some other of the Patriarchs who lived before the flood, have we all sinned? Would the learned man prove the consequence? Or what could he answer that could not be likewise answered to him? There is therefore no consequence. For by what art will the imputation of the first actual sin be elicited from there rather than of following sins, and of Adam's rather than of Seth's or Noah's, and antecedent rather than consequent? But, that I may act liberally, I confess that we have sinned in Adam's loins: does it therefore follow that his first actual sin is imputed to us by an imputation which precedes hereditary corruption? The contrary rather follows. For we have sinned in Adam, because we were in him. But we were in him as branches in a root. And branches are so in a root that nothing of the root is properly imputed to the branches, but the branches draw from the root their nature and vital sap, such as is in the root, good or bad. So we have drawn a corrupt nature from corrupt Adam. For the rest, neither was the mass properly in the firstfruits, but the firstfruits in the mass, nor other members in the head. And so these comparisons seem foreign from what we are doing, and induce no imputation, much less an immediate or antecedent one.

source_text:
VI. Sed nescio quid subiicit probationis. Erat quippe is persona publica et totum genus humanum repraesentabat longe efficacius quam summus Sacerdos in sanctuario totam gentem Israeliticam. Primum, nonne id aeque facile negari a me potest, ac affirmatur a viro docto? Deinde, fac ita esse, an igitur una aliqua, eaque prima, summi Sacerdotis actio genti Israeliticae imputabatur? Si ais, da locum Scripturae qui id doceat. Si negas, quid hoc facit ad probandam imputationem solius primi peccati actualis Adami, et quidem antecedentem? Repraesentabat populum Israeliticum summus sacerdos ex munere, ut vas foederis legalis, eumque super humeris et corde, quodammodo gestabat. Diciturne tale quid de Adamo?

VII. Nec minus, inquit, verum est, nos in Adamo peccasse, adeoque iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad poenam imputari, quam postea nos concrucifixos Christo in ipso satisfecisse iustitiae divinae, adeoque merito eius satisfactionem et obedientiam nobis imputari apud Deum ad iustitiam. Fateor nos in Adamo peccasse, et iuste nobis omnibus eius peccatum ad poenam imputari. Sed id nunc quidem inter nos non versatur in quaestione. Quaeritur tantum de imputationis modo, seu, ut ita loquar, specie: utrum antecedenter seu immediate imputetur, an mediante corruptione? Hoc affirmo, illud vir Clar. probare, nec conatur quidem. Aberrat igitur a statu quaestionis, quae inter ipsum et Placeum esse debebat. Ceterum in Christo satisfecisse iustitiae divinae dicimur, tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro satisfecit, cum is pro se satisfacere nullo modo deberet. Dicemurne similiter peccasse nos in Adamo tanquam in vade nostro, qui loco nostro peccasset? Scilicet nos tunc tenebamur Deo parere, Adamus non item. Ille autem in locum nostrum venit, ut nostro loco legem violaret. Hoccine placet viro celeberrimo? non arbitror. Iam autem observavi satisfactionem Christi nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro seu fide: itaque nihil ex illa comparatione effici posse, nisi ad summum peccatum Adami nobis imputari mediante consensu nostro, qui habitualiter in vitio haereditario includitur: quae ipsissima Placei sententia est.

VIII. Ultimo loco hoc pugnat argumento. Atque haec peccati Adamici imputatio eo aequior est, quod sicut vitae conditionem et promissionem non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis posteris acceperat, si staret, ita debuit mortis reatum suo lapsu non sibi tantum, sed etiam suis omnibus contraxisse: nam ad quem pertinent commoda, ad eum quoque onera et incommoda pertinere aequissimum est. Quomodo intelligit Adamum vitae conditionem et promissionem non sibi tantum sed etiam suis posteris accepisse si staret? An sic, posteros Adami futuros fuisse sub eadem conditione et promissione vitae, sub qua erat Adamus, hoc est, perpetuo victuros, si Dei legem non violassent? Hoc verissimum est. Nam sub quo foedere sunt patres, sub eodem etiam eorum liberi sunt. An Adamum communicaturum cum posteris iustitiam suam originalem, quam conservasset, fuisse? Nihil verius, sed quid ista ad imputationem peccati Adamici, praesertim antecedentem? Peccato suo se privavit iustitia originali, et corruptionem contraxit, eamque privationem et corruptionem propagavit in posteros, et per eam suum mortis reatum. Quare, ut fuit sub lege peccati et mortis, sic liberos genuit similiter sub lege peccati et mortis. Communicavit enim cum illis suum peccatum, et per peccatum mortem. An denique intelligit, iustitiam Adami, si stetisset, omnibus eius posteris ad vitam aeternam imputandam fuisse? Primum hoc negat, et aliquot argumentis refellit D. Garissolius lib. de Imput. primi peccati cap. xv. §. 14. pag. 510. 511. Deinde, unde id sciri potest? Denique, oportuisset Adamum gignere liberos sibi dissimiles, hoc est, immutabiles seu impeccabiles. Ponamus enim eos peccasse, fuissent simul et iusti imputatione paternae iustitiae, et iniusti proprio peccato, atque adeo simul et vita et morte digni. Si dixeris, peccando ab illa imputatione excidisse, reponam igitur illam imputationem superfluam ac inutilem fuisse, quippe quae, si peccassent, eis nullo fuisset usui; utpote non minus propria iustitia iustis, quam ipse fuerat Adamus. Valet igitur hoc argumentum ad evertendam potius quam ad stabiliendam imputationem antecedentem Adamici peccati. Quis enim credat, Deum aequissimum eam legem posuisse Adamo, ut si obediret, quantumvis constanter et perpetuo, non imputaretur eius obedientia posteris, imputaretur tamen eius inobedientia, si contingeret eum vel semel non obedire; atque ita (quod ad imputationem attinet) contrario modo sese obedientia et inobedientia haberent?
english: VI. But I do not know what proof he subjoins. For he was a public person, and represented the whole human race far more effectually than the high Priest in the sanctuary represented the whole Israelite nation. First, cannot that be denied by me as easily as it is affirmed by the learned man? Next, grant it is so — was therefore some one, and that the first, action of the high Priest imputed to the Israelite nation? If you say yes, give a place of Scripture that teaches it. If you deny, what does this do toward proving the imputation of Adam's first actual sin alone, and that antecedent? The high priest represented the Israelite people by office, as vessel of the legal covenant, and in a manner bore him upon shoulders and heart. Is anything of that kind said of Adam? VII. Nor is it less true, he says, that we have sinned in Adam, and so his sin is justly imputed to us all for punishment, than that afterward we, crucified together with Christ, have satisfied divine justice in him, and so his satisfaction and obedience are deservedly imputed to us before God for righteousness. I confess that we have sinned in Adam, and that his sin is justly imputed to us all for punishment. But that is not now in question between us. The question is only about the mode of imputation, or, so to speak, the species: whether it is imputed antecedently or immediately, or through corruption? This I affirm; that the distinguished man does not even try to prove. He therefore wanders from the state of the question which ought to have been between him and Placeus. For the rest, we are said to have satisfied divine justice in Christ as in our surety, who satisfied in our place, when he ought in no way to satisfy for himself. Shall we say likewise that we have sinned in Adam as in our surety, who would have sinned in our place? To be sure, we were then bound to obey God, Adam not likewise. And he came into our place, that he might violate the law in our place. Does this please the most celebrated man? I do not think so. And I have already observed that Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us through our consent or faith: and so nothing can be made of that comparison, except at most that Adam's sin is imputed to us through our consent, which is habitually included in hereditary vice: which is Placeus's very own judgment. VIII. In the last place he fights with this argument. And this imputation of Adam's sin is so much the fairer, because as he had received the condition and promise of life not for himself only but also for his posterity if he stood, so he ought by his fall to have contracted the guilt of death not for himself only but also for all his: for it is most equal that to whom the advantages belong, to him the burdens and disadvantages also belong. How does he understand that Adam had received the condition and promise of life not for himself only but also for his posterity if he stood? Thus — that Adam's posterity would have been under the same condition and promise of life under which Adam was, that is, would live forever if they had not violated God's law? This is most true. For under whatever covenant the fathers are, under the same their children also are. Or that Adam would have communicated to posterity his original righteousness which he had preserved? Nothing truer; but what is that to the imputation of Adam's sin, especially antecedent? By his sin he deprived himself of original righteousness, and contracted corruption, and propagated that privation and corruption into posterity, and through it his own guilt of death. So, as he was under the law of sin and death, so he begot children likewise under the law of sin and death. For he communicated to them his sin, and through sin death. Or finally does he understand that Adam's righteousness, if he had stood, would have been imputed to all his posterity for eternal life? First D. Garissoles denies this, and refutes it with several arguments, in the book on the Imputation of the first sin, chapter 15, section 14, pages 510–511. Next, whence can that be known? Finally, Adam would have had to beget children unlike himself, that is, immutable or impeccable. For let us suppose they sinned: they would have been at once both righteous by imputation of paternal righteousness and unrighteous by their own sin, and so at once worthy of both life and death. If you say they would have fallen from that imputation by sinning, I shall reply that that imputation would therefore have been superfluous and useless, inasmuch as, if they had sinned, it would have been of no use to them; seeing they would have been no less righteous by their own righteousness than Adam himself had been. This argument therefore avails rather to overturn than to establish the antecedent imputation of Adam's sin. For who would believe that the most equal God set Adam such a law, that if he obeyed, however constantly and perpetually, his obedience would not be imputed to posterity, yet his disobedience would be imputed if he happened even once not to obey; and so (as far as imputation is concerned) obedience and disobedience would stand in a contrary way?

source_text:
CAPUT VII.
Si quam imputationem primi Adae peccati probant Argumenta D. Garissolii, eam nonnisi mediatam seu consequentem esse.

I. Sic se habuerunt argumenta D. Maresii. Edita est Montalbani Anno M. DC. XLVIII. Decreti Synodici Carentonensis De Imputatione primi peccati Adae explicatio et defensio, autore Ant. Garissolio in Ecclesia et Academia Montalbanensi Verbi Dei ministro, et SS. Theologiae Professore; Amplissimis Ecclesiarum et Academiarum Tigurinae, Bernensis, Basileensis, Schaphusianae Praesidibus, supremisque Scholarchis etc. dicata, apud quos de quibusdam, quos non nominat, sparsit multa, et queritur, veritatis et pacis, suique adeo ipsius honoris causa, si quid intelligo, potius tacenda. Qui apud tantos viros tam publice accusati, sibi, nisi paci et tranquillitati Ecclesiae, quam famae suae, consultum maluissent, haudquaquam defuissent. Sed quia (quod mihi vehementer dolet) praematura morte magnus ille vir ereptus Ecclesiae est, parcitum eius memoriae, quantum possum, cupio.

II. Missa igitur Epistola dedicatoria, is toto fere libro duo quaedam manuscripta, Placeique theses refellere studuit. Eorum Manuscriptorum alterum prius, alterum posterius appellat, credo quia alterum ante Synodum nationalem, alterum post scriptum fuit. Prius illud paucis ante Synodum nationalem mensibus suus auctor ab amico pastore satis grandaevo rogatus ex tempore quasi fuderat, autographumque suum, quia tabellarius urgebat, nullo retento exemplari, nec cum ullo vel collega, vel amico communicatum, nec postea a se ullo modo visum, ad eum miserat. Itaque si qua illius disseminata sunt exemplaria, id, aut ab eo, ad quem missum fuerat, aut ab ipso D. Garissolio, cum quo ille id communicaverat, factum fuisse oportuit. Illud certe nec suus autor habet, neque Placeus, et quis illius aliquod habeat exemplar, nunc quidem me prorsus fugit. Itaque non possum illud cum D. Garissolii refutatione ullo modo conferre.

Ad posterius manuscriptum quod spectat, scriptum fuit a Placeo festinanti calamo ineunte anno 1647. nihilque est nisi responsio ad aliud manuscriptum ipsius Thesibus oppositum, ab amico quodam ipsi ob aetatem, et doctrinam et munus venerandum, compositum, et ad ipsum, ut ei, si minus acquiesceret, celeriter responderet, missum. Paruit ei Placeus, et respondit. Pervenit ad manus D. Garissolii ea responsio. Putavit eam manuscriptam et privatam una cum priore illo manuscripto publice, libro typis excuso, et apud Reverendos Helvetios, qui fortasse ne fando quidem quicquam de ea acceperant, sibi esse refutandam: quam, si una cum refutatione sua vulgasset, virisque amplissimis legendam exhibuisset, facillimum fuisset eis de tota hac causa iudicium ferre. Sed placuit viro docto Adversarium suum, (si tamen Adversarius appellandus est is, qui, ne verbo quidem, eum offendere cuperet) intra privatos parietes conclusum tenere, ac velut immisso lupatho coercere, dum foris, omnibus audientibus, apud illustrissimos viros, eum gravissime accusaret, causamque istam totam adversus eum disceptaret.

Ita autem duo illa manuscripta citat, quasi ab eodem autore conscripta essent, cum tamen non ignoraret solius posterioris Placeum esse autorem; id quod etiam uno aut altero loco non obscure innuit. Et cum posterius hoc manuscriptum in capita XIV. esset distributum, extractas ex eo particulas ubique fere disseminat, capite nunquam notato; ut nescias ex quo manuscripto, vel manuscripti capite excerptum sit id quod citat et refutat: quae res mihi manuscriptum posterius (illud enim prius, ut dixi, nec habeo, nec unde habere possim scio) cum eius refutatione conferenti, plurimum dedit negotii.

Quoniam autem in eo manuscripto Placeus primum statum quaestionis constituerat perquam accurate, deinde argumenta eius pro imputatione immediata peccati Adamici quicum disputabat, a Scriptura, a ratione, a Patrum et Reformatorum testimoniis ducta dissolverat, suamque responsionem variis contra illam imputationem, ut ferebat occasio, rationibus consparserat, exagitavit D. Garissolius vehementer illam status quaestionis constitutionem atque expositionem, eaque neglecta sententiam Placeo, quam non agnoscit, ubique attribuit, eamque argumentis ita oppugnavit, ut passim aliquas vel responsiones vel rationes Placei inseruerit, et refellere studuerit. Argumenta autem illius, cui Placeus respondebat, quam vim habeant, non aliunde melius cognosci potest quam ex manuscripto illo posteriore, in quo diligenter et summa cum fide ad rationis examen sunt revocata. Argumenta vero D. Gar. vel eadem sunt cum illis, vel, si ab illis aliquo modo differunt verbis et modo proponendi, idem tamen fere est pondus, ut vix a Manuscriptorum illius cum libro D. Gar. collatione et contentione eximi possint. Eximam tamen quoad potero, et hoc in loco lectori meo sistam, ut videat ea nihil antecedentem imputationem iuvare.

Ille igitur constituto, non ut voluit Placeus, sed ut ipse contra verba et mentem Placei voluit, statu quaestionis absque ulla imputationis distinctione, quoniam satis intelligebat, imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam per se ipsam probari nullo modo posse, statim digressus est totis quatuor capitibus IV. V. VI. VII. ut probaret in genere, imputationem alieni peccati iniustam non esse. Id quod primum non tam argumentari est quam respondere Argumento, quo imputatio antecedens primi Adae peccati impugnatur, ex eo ducto, quod illa videatur cum iustitia pugnare. Deinde id probat quod Placeus non negat. Qui enim imputationem agnoscit peccati alieni mediatam seu consequentem, is certe fatetur aliquam imputationem alieni peccati iniustam non esse. Non igitur in genere probandum id erat de alieni peccati imputatione; constat enim et iustam et iniustam esse aliquam posse; sed in specie de tali imputatione, qualis ponitur esse imputatio peccati Adami antecedens seu immediata. Id quod profecto probatu prorsus impossibile est. Sed quicquid sit, nunc enim mihi non libet cum viro docto excurrere, haec nulla est consequentia: Aliqua imputatio alieni peccati non est iniusta, Ergo primum peccatum actuale Adami omnibus eius posteris imputatur, et quidem imputatione corruptionem haereditariam antecedente. Non enim ex illo antecedente consequitur magis talis peccati, nempe primi actualis Adami, talis imputatio, nimirum antecedens, quam cuiusvis alius peccati alieni, sive ipsius Adami, sive aliorum Patriarcharum quaelibet imputatio.

Missa igitur illa digressione cap. viii. Argumenta quaedam profert ex cap. v. Ep. ad Rom. vss. 12. et seqq. Sed ea argumenta non probare nisi imputationem, quae corruptionem haereditariam consequitur, Primum ipse met fatetur, cap. 8. §. 3. p. 206. et alibi, ut est a nobis observatum supra cap. 4. p. 21. et cap. proximo p. 35.

Deinde cum sint ducta a comparatione, quam instituit Apostolus inter Christum et Adamum, posset iis omnibus una responsio opponi, nimirum similitudinem in re tantum esse non in rei modo. Quam responsionem Placeus non didicit a Socino, sed ab Apostolo Rom. 5. 15. 16. a Calvino Com. in Rom. 5. 17. et, ut alios omittam, a Clariss. Theologo Andrea Riveto, cuius haec sunt verba in Catholico Orthodoxo Tract. IV. Quaest. 2. §. 18. Nihil tamen est in hoc argumento quod nos adigat ut agnoscamus necessitatem qualitatum inhaerentium. Id enim probari tantum potest, nos in Christo iustitiam habere, quemadmodum in Adamo iniustitiam. Erit autem comparatio causarum, non modi quo nobis res communicatur. Nam peccatum Adami nobis communicatur per generationem, iustitia autem Christi per imputationem.
english: Chapter Seven. If the Arguments of D. Garissoles prove any imputation of Adam's first sin, that it is only mediate or consequent.

I. So stood the arguments of D. Maresius. There was published at Montauban in the year 1648 An Explanation and Defense of the Synodical Decree of Charenton On the Imputation of Adam's first sin, by Antoine Garissoles, minister of the Word of God in the Church and Academy of Montauban, and Professor of Sacred Theology; dedicated to the most ample Presidents and supreme Scholarchs of the Churches and Academies of Zurich, Bern, Basel, and Schaffhausen, among whom he scattered many things about certain persons whom he does not name, and complains of things which, if I understand anything, rather ought to have been silenced for the sake of truth and peace, and of his own honor. Those who were so publicly accused before such great men would by no means have failed themselves, unless they had preferred to consult the peace and tranquility of the Church rather than their own reputation. But because (which grieves me exceedingly) that great man was snatched from the Church by an early death, I desire that his memory be spared as far as I can.

II. The dedicatory Epistle therefore set aside, he nearly in the whole book studied to refute two certain manuscripts, and Placeus's theses. Of those Manuscripts he calls one prior, the other posterior, I believe because one was written before the National Synod, the other after. The prior, a few months before the National Synod, its author, asked by a pastor friend old enough, had poured out as it were on the spot, and had sent his autograph to him, because the courier was pressing, with no copy retained, nor shared with any colleague or friend, nor afterward seen by himself in any way. And so if any copies of it have been scattered, that must have been done either by him to whom it had been sent, or by D. Garissoles himself, with whom that man had shared it. That manuscript certainly neither its own author has, nor Placeus, and who has any copy of it now wholly escapes me. And so I cannot in any way compare it with D. Garissoles's refutation.

As to the later manuscript, it was written by Placeus with a hastening pen at the beginning of the year 1647, and is nothing but a reply to another manuscript opposed to his own Theses, composed by a certain friend venerable to him for age and doctrine and office, and sent to him that he might reply quickly if he did not rest in it. Placeus obeyed him, and replied. That reply came to D. Garissoles's hands. He thought that that manuscript and private writing, together with that prior manuscript, ought to be refuted by him publicly, in a book printed, and before the Reverend Swiss, who perhaps had not received even by hearsay anything about it: which, if he had published together with his refutation, and had set it before those most ample men to be read, it would have been most easy for them to pass judgment on this whole cause. But it pleased the learned man to keep his Adversary (if yet he is to be called Adversary who desired to offend him not even by a word) shut within private walls, and as it were to restrain him by a dock put in, while outdoors, with all hearing, before most illustrious men, he accused him most heavily, and disputed that whole cause against him.

And he so cites those two manuscripts as if they had been written by the same author, when yet he was not unaware that Placeus was author of the later only; which he also hints not obscurely in one or two places. And when this later manuscript had been distributed into fourteen chapters, he scatters particles extracted from it almost everywhere, with the chapter never marked, so that you do not know from which manuscript, or chapter of the manuscript, that which he cites and refutes has been excerpted: which matter gave me very much trouble when comparing the later manuscript (for that prior one, as I said, I neither have, nor know whence I could have it) with its refutation.

But since in that manuscript Placeus had first constituted the state of the question very accurately, then had dissolved his arguments for the immediate imputation of Adam's sin with whom he was disputing, drawn from Scripture, from reason, from the testimonies of the Fathers and of the Reformers, and had sprinkled his own reply with various reasons against that imputation as occasion offered, D. Garissoles vehemently harassed that constitution and exposition of the state of the question, and when that was neglected attributed to Placeus a judgment which he does not own, and so opposed it with arguments that he everywhere inserted some replies or reasons of Placeus and studied to refute them. But how much force those arguments have to which Placeus was replying can be known from nowhere better than from that later manuscript, in which they have been carefully and with greatest faithfulness recalled to the examination of reason. But D. Garissoles's arguments are either the same as those, or, if they differ from them somehow in words and in the manner of proposing, yet the weight is nearly the same, so that they can scarcely be exempted from a comparison and contention of that Manuscript with D. Garissoles's book. I will nevertheless exempt them as far as I can, and will set them before my reader in this place, that he may see that they help antecedent imputation nothing.

He therefore, having constituted the state of the question not as Placeus wished, but as he himself wished against Placeus's words and mind, without any distinction of imputation, since he understood well enough that antecedent or immediate imputation can in no way be proved by itself, at once digressed through four whole chapters, 4, 5, 6, and 7, to prove in general that the imputation of another's sin is not unjust. Which first is not so much to argue as to answer an Argument by which the antecedent imputation of Adam's first sin is attacked, drawn from this, that it seems to fight with justice. Next he proves what Placeus does not deny. For he who acknowledges a mediate or consequent imputation of another's sin certainly confesses that some imputation of another's sin is not unjust. Therefore that was not to be proved in general concerning the imputation of another's sin; for it is clear that there can be both a just and an unjust one; but in species concerning such an imputation as the antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's sin is posited to be. Which is indeed altogether impossible to prove. But whatever it be — for now I do not wish to digress with the learned man — this is no consequence: Some imputation of another's sin is not unjust; Therefore Adam's first actual sin is imputed to all his posterity, and that by an imputation preceding hereditary corruption. For from that antecedent there does not follow such an imputation of such a sin, namely Adam's first actual sin, namely an antecedent one, any more than any imputation whatever of any other alien sin, whether of Adam himself or of other Patriarchs.

That digression therefore dismissed, in chapter 8 he brings forth certain Arguments from chapter 5 of the Epistle to the Romans, verses 12 and following. But those arguments prove only an imputation which follows hereditary corruption. First he himself confesses it, chapter 8, section 3, page 206, and elsewhere, as has been observed by us above in chapter 4, page 21, and in the last chapter, page 35.

Next, since they are drawn from the comparison which the Apostle institutes between Christ and Adam, one reply could be set against them all, namely that the likeness is in the thing only, not in the mode of the thing. Which reply Placeus did not learn from Socinus, but from the Apostle, Romans 5:15–16, from Calvin's Commentary on Romans 5:17, and, to omit others, from the most distinguished theologian Andreas Rivetus, whose words these are in the Catholic Orthodox, Tractate IV, Question 2, section 18: There is nothing in this argument, however, that forces us to acknowledge a necessity of inhering qualities. For this only can be proved, that we have righteousness in Christ, just as injustice in Adam. But it will be a comparison of causes, not of the mode by which the thing is communicated to us. For Adam's sin is communicated to us by generation, but Christ's righteousness by imputation.

source_text:
Itaque non comparat Apostolus modos quibus iustitia recipitur, sed causas, effectus et subiecta utriusque. Causa salutis est obedientia secundi Adami, ut causa condemnationis fuit inobedientia primi. Effecta sunt quod una nos iniustos constituit, altera iustos. Subiecta sunt multi, per unum iusti, per alium iniusti redditi. Ideo Episcopus Bipontinus eiusdem cap. haec verba explicans, Sed non sicut delictum, ita et donum, Ex sola praecedenti similitudine concludit, Similitudo igitur est quoad rem inter haec, sed non quoad modum. Quocum ita sit, adversariorum claudicat argumentum, quia a re ad modum rei non bene argumentantur. In edit. Gall. §. 8. haec ultima verba efferuntur plenius: Cela estant, l'argument des Adversaires ne vaut rien; pource qu'ils concluent en iceluy, que nous sommes iustifiez en Christ de mesme facon que nous sommes rendus pecheurs en Adam, ce que l'Apostre ne dit pas.

Quid pro ista nostra responsione, et contra argumenta D. Gar. dici potuit disertius? Ea tamen expendamus breviter. Non referam omnia eius verba: sunt enim nimis prolixa; sed ea tantum, in quibus nervus et vis argumenti consistit.

Arg. I. Apostolus id sibi propositum habet posteriori capitis 5. parte, quae a vers. 12. usque ad finem pertingit, ut, quae de iustificatione docuit, ea nobilis typi expositione confirmet. Docuit autem cap. 4. iustificationis nostrae rationem in eo consistere, quod per imputationem iustitiae Christi fide perceptae, iustificemur, id est, iusti habeamur et absolvamur apud Deum etc. Itaque hoc vult Apostolus ex ista Christi cum Adamo collatione concludere, iustificationem nobis obtingere ex imputatione iustitiae Christi. Atqui hoc nulla legitima ratione concludi posset, nisi poneretur imputatio peccati Adae etc. Quae enim est eiusmodi consequentiae vis aut ratio? Peccatum naturaliter ex Adamo in nos propagatur, sine omni imputatione. Ergo iustitia secundi Adami, qui Christus est, non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit.

Resp. 1. Primam illam Maiorem propositionem, Apostolus quae de iustificatione cap. 4. docuit, ea nobilis typi expositione confirmat, vel universaliter accipi, vel particulariter; hoc est, Apostolum vel omnia quae docuit confirmare, vel quaedam. Si prius, falsa est propositio. Docuerat enim, fidem imputari ad iustitiam, non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, promissionem non esse per legem, quanam sit fides per quam iustificamur etc. Quae tamen proprie non confirmat ductis ab isto typo argumentis: quippe quorum in illa comparatione ne meminit quidem. Si posterius, vitiosum est argumentum, nec ullam concludendi vim habet: est enim in prima syllogismorum figura. Quod si concipiatur in tertia figura subiuncta minore universali; ea minor sine dubio falsa erit aperte.
english: Therefore the Apostle does not compare the modes by which righteousness is received, but the causes, effects, and subjects of each. The cause of salvation is the obedience of the second Adam, as the cause of condemnation was the disobedience of the first. The effects are that the one constitutes us unjust, the other just. The subjects are many, made just through the one, unjust through the other. Therefore the Bishop of Deux-Ponts, explaining these words of the same chapter, But not as the offense, so also the gift, concludes from the preceding likeness alone: The likeness, then, is as to the thing between these, but not as to the mode. Which being so, the adversaries' argument limps, because they do not argue well from the thing to the mode of the thing. In the French edition, section 8, these last words are set out more fully: That being so, the adversaries' argument is worth nothing; because they conclude therein that we are justified in Christ in the same fashion that we are made sinners in Adam, which the Apostle does not say.

What could have been said more clearly for this our reply, and against the arguments of D. Garissoles? Yet let us weigh them briefly. I will not report all his words: for they are too prolix; but only those in which the nerve and force of the argument consists.

Arg. I. The Apostle has this proposed to himself in the latter part of chapter 5, which extends from verse 12 to the end, that what he taught concerning justification he may confirm by exposition of a noble type. But he taught in chapter 4 that the reason of our justification consists in this, that through the imputation of Christ's righteousness received by faith we are justified, that is, are held just and are absolved before God, etc. Therefore the Apostle wants to conclude from that comparison of Christ with Adam that justification befalls us from the imputation of Christ's righteousness. And yet this could be concluded by no legitimate reason unless the imputation of Adam's sin were posited, etc. For what is the force or reason of a consequence of that kind? Sin is propagated naturally from Adam into us, without any imputation. Therefore the righteousness of the second Adam, who is Christ, descends to us not by propagation but by imputation.

Reply 1. That first Major proposition — The Apostle confirms by exposition of a noble type what he taught concerning justification in chapter 4 — is taken either universally or particularly; that is, that the Apostle confirms either all things which he taught, or some. If the former, the proposition is false. For he had taught that faith is imputed unto righteousness, that a man is not justified from the works of the law, that the promise is not through the law, what faith that is through which we are justified, etc. Which things, however, he does not properly confirm by arguments drawn from that type: inasmuch as of them he does not even make mention in that comparison. If the latter, the argument is vicious and has no force of concluding: for it is in the first figure of syllogisms. And if it be conceived in the third figure with a universal minor joined, that minor will without doubt be openly false.

source_text:
Resp. 2. Ut ponamus vitio carere Syllogismum, eius conclusionem non obesse Placeo. Concedit enim ultro primi Adae peccati imputationem, modo consequens seu mediata intelligatur, quam intelligi, non autem antecedentem seu immediatam, illa ipsa Christum inter et Adamum comparatio flagitat. Nam imputatio iustitiae Christi fide perceptae, nostrum consensum, nostram fidem consequitur, eaque mediante fit. Consentaneum est igitur, ut imputatio primi Adae peccati ei respondens, aliquem nostrum, si non actum, saltem habitum, si non actualem, saltem habitualem consensum sequatur, eoque mediante fiat.

Resp. 3. eam D. Gar. conclusionem adscribere Apostolo, quae ex illa comparatione deduci non potest, nisi eversa constante omnium Patrum, omniumque Ecclesiarum Orthodoxarum doctrina. Vult enim hanc esse conclusionem Apostoli. Ergo iustitia secundi Adami, qui Christus est, non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit. Quae conclusio sequi non potest nisi ex hoc antecedente, Peccatum Adami non propagatione, sed imputatione ad nos descendit. Nam si ponas peccatum Adami partim propagatione, partim imputatione ad nos descendere, qua consequentia inde conficies, iustitiam Christi non propagatione, sed imputatione descendere? Oportet certe similiter in antecedente propagationem peccati Adae negare, quam omnes et Patres et Protestantes constanter docuerunt. Quid, quod etiam posito isto falso et erroneo antecedente, consequi non potest illa conclusio, nisi vi maioris istius propositionis quam subticuit, Quomodo peccatum Adami ad nos descendit, eodem, et non alio, descendit ad nos Christi iustitia. Iam autem ista propositio si ita universaliter intelligitur, aperte falsa est. Descendit enim in nos peccatum Adami non ex gratia, sed ex iustitia; naturaliter, non supernaturaliter; nobis actu non consentientibus etc. Eodemne modo descendit ad nos Christi iustitia? Sin autem intelligitur particulariter, ut sit similitudo in quodam modo, non in omni, vitiosa erit consequentia, ut pote ex maiore particulari in prima figura. It ergo et contra Ecclesiae doctrinam haec argumentatio, et Apostolum facit male ratiocinantem. Quae omnia viro docto excidisse, et quidem in ipso primo eius argumento, dolendum profecto est, ut et illud quod sequitur.
english: Reply 2. Grant that the Syllogism is free of fault: its conclusion does not hurt Placeus. For he freely grants the imputation of Adam's first sin, provided the consequent or mediate be understood — which that very comparison between Christ and Adam demands to be understood, not the antecedent or immediate. For the imputation of Christ's righteousness received by faith follows our consent, our faith, and is made by that mediating. It is therefore fitting that the imputation of Adam's first sin answering to it should follow some consent of ours — if not an act, at least a habit; if not actual, at least habitual — and be made by that mediating.

Reply 3. To ascribe to the Apostle that conclusion of D. Garissoles which cannot be drawn from that comparison unless the constant doctrine of all the Fathers and of all the Orthodox Churches is overturned. For he wants this to be the Apostle's conclusion: Therefore the righteousness of the second Adam, who is Christ, descends to us not by propagation but by imputation. Which conclusion cannot follow except from this antecedent: Adam's sin descends to us not by propagation but by imputation. For if you posit that Adam's sin descends to us partly by propagation, partly by imputation, by what consequence will you thence make out that Christ's righteousness descends not by propagation but by imputation? Certainly you must likewise deny in the antecedent the propagation of Adam's sin, which all both Fathers and Protestants have constantly taught. What of this — that even with that false and erroneous antecedent posited, that conclusion cannot follow except by force of that greater proposition which he suppressed: In whatever way Adam's sin descends to us, in the same way, and not another, Christ's righteousness descends to us. But now if that proposition is understood so universally, it is openly false. For Adam's sin descends into us not from grace but from justice; naturally, not supernaturally; with us not actually consenting, etc. Does Christ's righteousness descend to us in the same way? But if it is understood particularly, so that there is likeness in a certain mode, not in every, the consequence will be vicious, as from a particular major in the first figure. This argumentation therefore both goes against the Church's doctrine and makes the Apostle reason badly. Which things all fell from the learned man, and that in his very first argument — truly to be lamented — as also that which follows.

source_text: Alterum hoc, inquit, rectissime et evidentissime concluditur: Adamus est typus Christi, et sunt Adamus et Christus capita generis humani in contrariis effectis. Atqui Adamici peccati imputatione omnes sumus peccatores et rei. Ergo et iustitiae Christi imputatione omnes iustificamur, seu iusti constituimur apud Deum. Quomodo enim id rectissime et evidentissime concluditur, cum sint in argumento sex aut septem termini? Et quomodo hoc voluit concludere Apostolus, qui neque imputationis peccati Adamici, neque imputationis iustitiae Christi in toto hoc capite meminit? Et quomodo si hoc Apostolus voluit, Calvinus, Martyr, et alii in suis commentariis, eius mentem et verba exposuerunt, nulla, neque imputationis peccati Adami, neque eiusmodi argumentationis, facta mentione? Quid, quod istud argumentum, adeo non rectissime et evidentissime concludit, ut etiam possit retorqueri. Nam quae est consequentia, Adamus et Christus sunt capita generis humani in contrariis effectis. Ergo contraria ista effecta ab iis eodem prorsus modo procedunt? Annon potius sequitur, contraria cum sint effecta, illa ab iis contrario modo procedere? id quod etiam res ipsa confirmat. Nam ab Adamo nascimur peccatores naturaliter, a Christo sumus iusti supernaturaliter, ab illo ex iustitia, ab hoc ex gratia, ab illo sine actuali nostro consensu, ab hoc per actualem nostrum consensum, ab illo per propagationem naturalem, (id enim ex quo nata est haeresis Pelagiana perpetuo ab orthodoxis creditum fuit.) ab hoc nullo modo per eiusmodi propagationem. Mitto cetera discrimina, quorum quaedam, ut dixi, ipse Apostolus observavit, quaedam Calvinus ad vers. 17. iis, quae Apostolus observaverat, adiunxit. Sed fac argumentum illud D. Gar. recte concludere, concedet Placeus nos omnes Adamici peccati imputatione consequente seu mediata esse peccatores et reos, negabit antecedente seu immediata. Quid facilius quam ita respondere?
english: This second [argument], he says, is concluded most rightly and most evidently: Adam is the type of Christ, and Adam and Christ are heads of the human race in contrary effects. And yet by the imputation of Adam's sin we all are sinners and guilty. Therefore also by the imputation of Christ's righteousness we all are justified, or are constituted just before God. How indeed is that concluded most rightly and most evidently, when there are in the argument six or seven terms? And how did the Apostle want to conclude this, who in this whole chapter mentions neither the imputation of Adam's sin nor the imputation of Christ's righteousness? And how, if the Apostle wanted this, did Calvin, Martyr, and others in their commentaries expound his mind and words, with no mention made either of the imputation of Adam's sin or of an argumentation of that kind? What of this — that that argument so little concludes most rightly and most evidently that it can even be turned back. For what is the consequence: Adam and Christ are heads of the human race in contrary effects. Therefore those contrary effects proceed from them in altogether the same mode? Does it not rather follow that, since the effects are contrary, they proceed from them in a contrary mode? which the thing itself also confirms. For from Adam we are born sinners naturally; from Christ we are just supernaturally; from him by justice, from this by grace; from him without our actual consent, from this through our actual consent; from him by natural propagation (for that, from which the Pelagian heresy was born, has been perpetually believed by the orthodox), from this in no way by such propagation. I pass over the other differences, of which some, as I said, the Apostle himself observed, some Calvin at verse 17 joined to those which the Apostle had observed. But grant that that argument of D. Garissoles concludes rightly: Placeus will concede that we all are sinners and guilty by consequent or mediate imputation of Adam's sin; he will deny by antecedent or immediate. What is easier than so to reply?

source_text:
Hic D. G. laudato loco ex Clar. Amyraldi lib. de Iustif. in Millet. c. 3. ex eo sic colligit. Audis, inquit, ex inobedientia Adami, quae fuerit unica actio, in nos descendentem condemnationem, quae non sit aliquid inhaerens, sed obligatio ad poenam (addiderat Cl. Amyr. vel obligationis illius declaratio a potestate superiori). Qui autem propter inobedientiam alterius obligatur ad poenam, reatum sustinet illius inobedientiae, adeoque imputatur ei illa inobedientia.

Audio quidem ex illa inobedientia descendere in nos condemnationem, sed non audio descendere immediate et ante corruptionem haereditariam: id quod tamen unum inter nos controversitur. Dixit vir Clar. Adamum inobedientia sua condemnationem et mortem invexisse, nimirum quia invexit peccatum in omnes homines, causam condemnationis et mortis, ut patet ex Rom. 5. 12. Dixit eos qui cum Adamo communionem habent, eius condemnationem participare, et una cum eo morte esse subiectos. Intelligit autem communionem cum Adamo, non quatenus fuit homo (hanc enim etiam ipse Christus habuit) sed quatenus fuit peccator. Habemus autem communionem cum Adamo quatenus fuit homo, quia traximus ab eo naturam nostram, et quatenus fuit peccator, quia traximus ab eo peccatum nostrum. Sustinemus itaque reatum illius inobedientiae, sed mediante corruptione ab eo in nos derivata.
english: Here D. Garissoles, at the place praised, from the distinguished Amyraut's book On Justification in the Milletus, chapter 3, gathers thus from him. You hear, he says, a condemnation descending into us from Adam's disobedience, which was a single action — a condemnation which is not something inhering, but an obligation to punishment (the distinguished Amyraut had added: or a declaration of that obligation by a superior power). But he who on account of another's disobedience is obligated to punishment sustains the guilt of that disobedience, and so that disobedience is imputed to him.

I do indeed hear condemnation descending into us from that disobedience, but I do not hear it descending immediately and before hereditary corruption: which yet is the one thing controverted between us. The distinguished man said that Adam by his disobedience brought in condemnation and death, namely because he brought in sin into all men, the cause of condemnation and death, as is plain from Romans 5:12. He said that those who have communion with Adam share his condemnation and together with him have been subjected to death. But he understands communion with Adam not insofar as he was man (for even Christ himself had this) but insofar as he was a sinner.
