Thus in Adam what belongs to sin and nature stands out, and in the rest what belongs to God's providence and grace.

source_text: Quaerenti ergo, unde fit, ut parentes, qui peccatis variis sese commaculant, inquinamenta illa peccatorum suorum non semper transmittant in liberos? Respondeo verbis Petri Martyris, quia Deus modum praefixit, ne malum grassetur in immensum, & hanc mali propagationem suspendit. Cur Adamus inobediens filios generat rebelles Deo, & natura contumaces? Respondeo, quia Deus voluit permittere, hoc est, non impedire lapsum Adami & lapsus propagationem. Cur Achas idololatra non generat Ezechiam sibi similem? Quia Deus, qui Ezechiam elegerat, eum a paterna idololatria Spiritus sancti virtute liberavit. Cur adulteri, ebriosi, praedones, non semper gignunt filios in eadem vitia praecipites? Quia vitia illa, vel non propagantur impediente Dei providentia, quae humani generis conservationi prospicit, vel propagata tolluntur regenerationis gratia.
english: Ask, then, why parents stained by many kinds of sin do not always pass those stains to their children. I answer with Peter Martyr: God fixed a bound so that evil would not rage without measure, and He held this spread of evil in suspension. Why does disobedient Adam still beget sons rebellious toward God and stubborn by nature? Because God willed to permit the fall — which is to say, not to stop Adam's fall or its onward spread. Why does idolatrous Ahaz fail to beget a Hezekiah in his own likeness? Because the God who had chosen Hezekiah loosed him from his father's idolatry by the Holy Spirit's power. And why do adulterers, drunkards, and robbers not always raise children rushing into the same vices? Either providence, watching over the human race's conservation, blocks those vices from spreading, or regenerating grace later strips away what did spread.

source_text: Itaque vitium tam vetus propagatur, quia Deus noluit quominus propagaretur impedire: non propagantur recentiora, quia Deus voluit ne propagarentur impedire. Uno verbo, voluit permittere propagationem lapsus Adami, non aliorum peccatorum. Vides, opinor jam aequissime Lector, nobis aquam nullo modo haerere. Aliam ejusmodi discriminis rationem Placeus cum in Thesibus, tum in Manuscripto posteriore reddiderat ab ipsa primi Adae peccati natura petitam, quae suo loco ab exceptionibus D. Garissolii Deo dante vindicabitur. Nunc enim mihi satis est ostendisse, quam ipse hujus discriminis rationem reddit, eam, non minus propagationi quam imputationi applicari posse: Estque nostra quam eius causa melior. Nihil enim sic respondendo dicimus quod possit negari. Convenit enim inter nos propagari peccatum originale, non perpetuo propagari alia vitia, nihilque fieri posse Deo prorsus inscio & invito. Ille vero sic respondendo, supponit imputationem antecedentem, quam nos negamus, & probare debebat, Deoque voluntatem sic imputandi primi Adae peccati actualis tribuit: quam tamen voluntatem Deus neque per naturam, neque per Scripturam patefecit. Id quod peccato vacare non videtur.
english: Hence the ancient vice spreads because God refused to stop it; the newer ones do not, because God chose to stop them. One word sums it: He permitted Adam's fall to propagate, not other sins. Fairest reader, you already see that we are not stuck for an answer. Another account of the same discrimination — drawn from the nature of Adam's first sin itself — Placeus had already given in the Theses and again in a later Manuscript; God willing, it will be cleared in its place from D. Garissoles's exceptions. What matters now is only this: the very reason Garissoles offers for the discrimination serves propagation no less than imputation, and our cause is the stronger. Our reply denies nothing agreed between us — that original sin does propagate, that other vices do not always, and that nothing occurs with God wholly unaware and unwilling. His reply, by contrast, quietly assumes the antecedent imputation we deny and that he was bound to prove, and it lays on God a will to impute Adam's first actual sin that neither nature nor Scripture has ever disclosed. That does not look free of sin.

source_text: Adde quod, si rei illius vera & solida, & unica causa est Dei voluntas, cui sic libuit nobis omnibus primum Adami peccatum imputare; nec libuit aut sequentia Adami, aut aliorum parentum peccata imputare, fatendum est (id quod vehementissime refugit conscientia) veram & solidam & unicam causam cur simus peccatores & perditi, Dei voluntatem esse, contra oraculum, Ex te perditio tua, o Israel. Fateor equidem cum propagatione vitii originalis imputationem, nisi Dei misericordia intercedat, cohaerere, sed ea imputatio sequitur propagationem, non antecedit, nec est ullo modo propagationis causa. At ponere imputationem, qua peccatum actuale Adami nostrum fiat, qua fiamus peccatores & rei mortis aeternae, quae sit causa propagationis peccati, & hujus imputationis unicam esse causam Dei voluntatem, quid est facere Deum perditionis nostrae autorem, si hoc non est?
english: There is more. If the true, solid, and only cause of that difference is God's will — pleased to charge Adam's first sin to us all, yet not pleased to charge Adam's later sins or the sins of other parents — then we must confess what conscience most fiercely flees: that the true, solid, and only cause of our being sinners and lost is God's will. That runs against the oracle, From you is your destruction, O Israel. I do admit that, where original vice propagates, an imputation hangs together with it unless mercy from God steps in; yet that imputation comes after the propagation, never before it, and never as its cause. But to plant an imputation that makes Adam's actual sin ours, that makes us sinners and debtors to eternal death, that is then treated as the cause of sin's spread, and whose only cause is said to be God's will — if that is not to cast God as the author of our perdition, what is?

source_text: Sed fortasse exigebat justitia, ut Deus vellet primum illud peccatum imputare potius quam alia peccata? Cur ergo, inquam, hanc causam non attulit? cur dixit illius rei unicam esse causam, Dei voluntatem? Aut quomodo probabitur (nos enim nunc quidem respondentium partes tuemur) id justitiam exegisse? Si confugias ad conjunctionem quae nobis cum Adamo intercedit, ea ne major fuit cum primum peccaret quam postea, aut cum eo, quam cum propinquioribus nostris parentibus? Si ad nescio quoddam foedus, cujus haec fuerit conditio, ut si peccaret, primum eius peccatum omnibus eius posteris ad duas istas poenas imputaretur, peccatum inhaerens & mortem aeternam, probandum erit illud foedus e Scriptura; id quod est prorsus impossibile. Cavendum est autem nobis quam diligentissime ne quid praeter Scripturam Deo tribuamus, praesertim ejusmodi, quod virtutes eius obscuret; id enim non potest non grave peccatum esse.
english: Someone may say justice itself required God to will the imputation of that first sin rather than of other sins. Then why, I ask, was that cause never produced? Why call God's will the unique cause of the matter? And how — while we for now only answer — will anyone prove that justice required it? Flee to our conjunction with Adam, and was that bond stronger at his first sin than later, or stronger with him than with parents nearer to us? Flee to some unknown covenant whose terms were that, if he sinned, his first sin would be charged to all his posterity under those two penalties — inherent sin and eternal death — and that covenant must be proved from Scripture, which cannot be done at all. Above all we must beware of ascribing to God anything Scripture does not give Him, especially anything that clouds His virtues; for that cannot fail to be a grave sin.

source_text: Hac ratione sic proposita Theologorum auxilium sibi adjungit, & Vitakerum, Chamierum, Sixtum Senensem, & Bellarminum nominat. Nostros cur laudet non miror: ita enim in hac causa usuvenit, novitatis suspicionem amoliendi causa: Sed cur Pontificios? cur Bellarminum? Nosne putavit eorum autoritate moveri posse? Non arbitror: Sed suis rationibus conjungere voluit ad nos oppugnandos Bellarmini rationes. Eum enim dicit non contemnendis ad firmandam hanc sententiam rationibus fultum procedere in medium lib. 5. de Amiss. Grat. & Stat. pecc. cap. 18. Age igitur hujus etiam solvamus rationes, eoque majore animo quod si quid intelligo, receptae in Ecclesiis nostris doctrinae de peccato originali non obscure adversantur.
english: With that argument laid out, Garissoles calls in the theologians' help and names Whitaker, Chamier, Sixtus of Siena, and Bellarmine. That he praises our writers does not surprise me: that is how this debate usually goes when novelty is the charge to be shaken off. But why the Papists? Why Bellarmine? Did he think their authority would move us? I do not think so. He meant to join Bellarmine's reasons to his own against us. He says Bellarmine comes forward on no contemptible grounds for confirming this opinion — book 5 of On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, chapter 18. Very well: let us answer those reasons too, and with the more spirit because, if I understand them, they cut plainly against the doctrine of original sin received in our churches.

source_text: Nisi ponamus, inquit, nos in Adamo, & cum Adamo vere peccasse, nulla ratione explicari poterit, quomodo in parvulis recens natis sit aliqua vera culpa, & hoc Catholicum dogma, non tam supra rationem, quam contra rationem esse videbitur. Antequam progrediamur, quid est in & cum Adamo peccare? Figuratam enim profecto locutionem esse oportet. Fortasse est nobis Adami peccatum imputari. Hoc posito, propositionem illam nego.
english: Unless we grant, he says, that we truly sinned in Adam and with Adam, there is no way to explain how newborn infants bear any true guilt, and this Catholic dogma will look not merely above reason but against it. Before we go further: what does it mean to sin in and with Adam? The phrase has to be figurative. Perhaps it means Adam's sin is imputed to us. Take that reading, and I deny the proposition.

source_text: Eam probat Bellarminus, Nam, inquit, quicquid dicamus in parvulis ex peccato haerere, sive reatum, sive aversionem, sive gratiae privationem, sive quid aliud; nullo modo parvulis vitio dari, ac ne esse quidem poterit, nisi processerit ab actione libera, cujus actionis illi aliquomodo participes fuerint. Nonne hoc est negare, vitium haereditarium, infantibus inhaerens, esse vere peccatum iis damnandis sufficiens, uti nostra pronunciat Confessio Artic. XI. Sed pergat. Nam primo, reatus, cum sit relatio consequens actionem, qui fieri potest ut existat in eo, qui non est particeps actionis? Valeret sane hoc argumentum, si nullum esset peccatum nisi actuale, nullus reatus nisi proxime actionem consequens. Nunc autem est etiam peccatum habituale, & reatus consequens habitum.
english: Bellarmine's proof runs: whatever we say clings in little children from sin — guilt, aversion, loss of grace, or anything else — cannot be vice in them, cannot even exist, unless it came from a free act in which they somehow shared. Is that not to deny that the hereditary blot in infants is truly sin enough to damn them, as our Confession states in Article XI? Let him continue. First: guilt is a relation that follows an act — how can it stand in someone who had no share in the act? The argument would hold if the only sin were actual sin, and the only guilt what follows an act at once. But there is also habitual sin, and guilt that follows a habit.

source_text: Secundo (recito enim has rationes ut apud D. Garissolium extant) aversio habitualis, nisi praecesserit actualis, ne intelligi quidem potest. Hoc vero insigniter falsum est, si actualis aversio ipsorum parvulorum intelligitur. Alioqui quis negat aversionem actualem Adami praecessisse habitualem in ipso, & hanc esse in parvulos propagatam? Profecto aversio a Deo, in quocunque sit, hoc ipso quod est aversio a Deo, peccatum est. Tertio, fingamus parvulum aliquem habere aversionem & reatum, & tamen non peccasse cum Adamo, quis capere poterit, eum merito reprehendi, & puniri debere. Quam culpam habet in eo, quod ita generatus est? Num impedire potuit, ne sic gigneretur?
english: Second — I recite the reasons as they stand in D. Garissoles — habitual aversion cannot even be conceived unless actual aversion went before. That is strikingly false if the actual aversion meant is the infants' own. Who denies that Adam's own actual turning from God preceded the habitual turn in him, and that this was passed down into the little ones? Aversion from God, wherever it is found, is sin simply because it is aversion from God. Third: imagine an infant who has aversion and guilt yet never sinned with Adam — how is he justly blamed and punished? What is his fault in being born so? Could he stop being begotten that way?

source_text: Ex mente D. Garissolii peccasse cum Adamo est peccatum imputari, & quidem imputatione vitium inhaerens antecedente: alioqui nos istae rationes non oppugnarent. Jam autem sublata ista imputatione, potestne aversio a Deo, in quocunque sit, non digna esse reprehensione? Culpa quidem eius non est quod ita generatus est, sed quod ita comparatus est, quod nequam, quod impius, quod Dei adversarius est, haec est profecto magna culpa, non quidem, ut loquuntur, culpa actualis, sed tamen habitualis. Ab actuali inobedientia causa a qua est, extrinsece; ab habituali vero subjectum in quo est, intrinsece denominatur inobediens. Non est igitur parvulus reus ab actione proxime sed ab habitu: non quia malam aliquam actionem commiserit, sed quia ipse malus est, & ad male agendum comparatus.
english: On Garissoles's reading, to have sinned with Adam means the sin is imputed, and imputed ahead of the inherent blot: otherwise those reasons would not touch us. But once that imputation is set aside, can aversion from God, in anyone, fail to deserve rebuke? The child's fault is not that he was born so, but that he is so constitutioned — base, godless, God's enemy. That is a great fault indeed: not actual guilt as they speak of it, yet habitual. From actual disobedience he is called disobedient from without, by the cause that produced it; from habitual disobedience, from within, by the subject that bears it. So the infant is not guilty from a nearby act but from a habit: not because he did some evil deed, but because he himself is evil and set for evil doing.

source_text: Quarto, non satis est ad culpam, ut aliquid sit voluntarium habituali voluntate, sed requiritur, ut processerit ab actu etiam voluntario; alioqui voluntarium illud voluntate habituali naturale esset, & misericordia, non reprehensione dignum. Immo inquam, id satis est ad culpam habitualem. Non enim vitium originale dicitur voluntarium, quia est a voluntate, sed quia est in voluntate: illo modo voluntarius est actus, isto habitus: Nimirum vitium illud est ipsius voluntatis malitia & pravitas, a qua, licet naturalis sit, mala dicitur. Quo magis autem naturaliter mala est voluntas, eo est pejor, & odio dignior.
english: Fourth: guilt is said to need more than voluntariness by habitual will; it must also have come from a voluntary act — otherwise that habitual voluntariness would be natural and fit for mercy, not for blame. I say the opposite: that is enough for habitual guilt. Original vice is called voluntary not because it comes from the will, but because it is in the will: the first way makes the act voluntary, the second the habit. That vice is the will's own malice and crookedness, and though natural it is still called evil. The more naturally evil the will, the worse it is, and the more hateful.

source_text: Caeterum quis non videt has rationes posse retorqueri? Reatus enim est relatio consequens actionem eius cujus est reatus, non autem alterius: & habitus sequi solet actionem eius cujus est habitus, non autem actionem alterius: Et, Num impedire potuimus, aut debuimus ne peccaret Adamus? Et, quomodo est voluntarium respectu voluntatis nostrae, quod tanto tempore, antequam ullam haberemus voluntatem factum est? Et, facit-ne illa imputatio, ut peccatum illud actuale Adami processerit ab actu voluntario nostro? aut sumus-ne minus necessario rei, quam corrupti? Num sumus commeriti, ut tales gigneremur? Legantur Theologi nostri, adversus vel Pelagium, vel Pighium, vel ipsum Bellarminum disputantes, praesertim cum tractant controversiam de peccato originali & concupiscentia, an sit peccatum, etiam post susceptum baptismum.
english: Besides, who cannot see these reasons turned back on themselves? Guilt follows the act of the person whose guilt it is, not someone else's; and habit usually follows that person's act, not another's. Could we — or should we — have stopped Adam from sinning? How is something voluntary with respect to our will if it was done long before we had any will at all? Does the imputation make Adam's actual sin proceed from our voluntary act? Are we any less necessarily guilty than corrupt? Did we earn being born this way? Read our own theologians against Pelagius, Pighius, or Bellarmine himself, especially where they ask whether original sin and concupiscence remain sin even after baptism.

source_text: Superest ultima eius ratio ducta ab imputatione Iustitiae Christi. Eam sic concipit. Quod doctrinam de imputata Christi justitia vel convellit, vel labefactat, neque admittendum, neque tolerandum est, sed amolendum omnino ac rejiciendum. Atqui dogmate de Non-imputatione peccati Adae, doctrinam de imputatione justitiae Christi, non parum labefactari certum est, cum ex negatione prioris facillimus sit lapsus ad posterioris negationem. Nam cum in Christo tanquam secundo Adamo, remedium habeamus certissimum adversus ea mala & damna, quae sunt in genus humanum a primo Adamo invecta; Remedium autem morbis, quibus sanandis paratum est, justa proportione respondere debeat; qui praeter nativam corruptionem, nihil nos damni ex Adamo trahere existimabit, & huic corruptioni considerabit ex adverso respondere donum sanctificationis, facile in eam sententiam deveniet, cum nullus sit in nobis propter Adae inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, neque opus esse ulla justitia Christi imputatione, quae sanctificationem ordine naturae praecedat: quia ubi nullum est malum, nullo etiam opus est remedio.
english: His last argument remains, drawn from the imputation of Christ’s justice. He puts it this way: anything that overturns or shakes the teaching of Christ’s imputed righteousness must not be allowed or endured, but must be rooted out and cast off entirely. Yet the dogma that Adam’s sin is not imputed, he says, certainly shakes that teaching more than a little — because denying the first makes denying the second an easy slide. Since in Christ, the second Adam, we have a sure remedy against the evils and losses the first Adam brought on the human race, and a remedy ought to match the diseases it is meant to heal, anyone who thinks we inherit from Adam nothing worse than native corruption — and who sets sanctification over against that corruption — will soon conclude that we have no guilt earlier than our original stain from Adam’s disobedience, and that we need no imputation of Christ’s justice ahead of sanctification in nature’s order: where there is no evil, no remedy is needed.

source_text: Nego dogma de Non-imputatione peccati Adae antecedente seu immediata ullo modo doctrinam de imputatione justitiae Christi labefactare; mihique valde dolet, quod videam virum doctum, ut id probet, deserere doctrinam de corruptionis nativae reatu, publicis fidei confessionibus Ecclesiarum protestantium declaratam, & confirmatam. Corruptio nativa duobus modis spectari potest: uno forensi, altero morali. Priori modo consideratur ut peccatum nobis damnandis sufficiens: Posteriori vero ut qualitas nos sua inhaerentia polluens. Quatenus est peccatum nos irae Dei addicens, ei respondet justificatio: quatenus vero est qualitas foeda nobis inhaerens, ei respondet sanctificatio. Tolli autem ista qualitas non potest, nisi prius tollatur ejus reatus. Itaque sanctificationem ordine naturae justificatio praecedit.
english: I deny that refusing antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam’s sin weakens, in any way, the doctrine of Christ’s imputed justice. It pains me to watch a learned man, for the sake of his proof, abandon the teaching that native corruption carries guilt — a teaching the Protestant churches have stated and sealed in their public confessions. Native corruption can be read two ways: forensically, or morally. Forensically it is sin enough to damn us; morally it is a quality that fouls us by clinging in us. As sin that binds us under God’s wrath, justification answers it; as a foul quality inhering in us, sanctification answers it. That quality cannot be removed until its guilt is removed first. So in nature’s order, justification comes before sanctification.

source_text: Cum igitur corruptio duplicem illum respectum habeat, unum forensem, quo fit, ut, nisi condonetur, imputetur ad mortem; alterum moralem seu philosophicum, quo subjectum reddit habile ad peccandum, duplici nobis remedio opus fuit, imputatione justitiae Christi, quae mederetur reatui corruptionis, & vi Spiritus, qua e subjecto revelleretur. Nonne orthodoxa est haec doctrina, & ab omnibus purioribus Ecclesiis confessa? Miror igitur eam doctrinam a D. Garissolio hoc loco fuisse negatam. Quanquam id non est admodum mirandum. Vix enim fieri potest, quin in hunc scopulum incurrant ij, qui antecedentem imputationem probare student.
english: Corruption therefore wears a double face: forensic — so that unless it is forgiven it is charged to death — and moral or philosophical, making the subject ready to sin. We therefore needed a double cure: Christ’s justice imputed to heal corruption’s guilt, and the Spirit’s power to tear the blot out of the subject. Is this not orthodox teaching, confessed by all the purer churches? I am astonished that D. Garissoles denied it here — though the astonishment should not run deep. Those who press antecedent imputation almost cannot help striking this reef.

source_text: Caeterum necessaria est imputatio justitiae non modo ut a reatu vitii inhaerentis, verum etiam ut ab omnibus aliis nostris peccatis justificemur. Id enim quod Deus gratificatur est ex multis lapsibus ad justificationem. Rom.5.16.
english: Moreover, the imputation of justice is needed not only to clear us of the guilt of the vice that inheres, but also to justify us from all our other sins. What God freely grants is justification from many falls (Rom. 5:16).

source_text: Possem etiam hanc rationem in suum autorem retorquere. Nam si ubi nullum est malum, nullo opus est remedio, & nullum sit malum, si nullus sit in nobis propter Adae inobedientiam reatus labe nostra originali prior, & cur sit in nobis iste reatus vera & unica causa est Dei voluntas, non intelligo quae sit imputatae justitiae necessitas. Abstineat modo Deus ab imputatione primi Adae peccati quemadmodum sibi temperat ab aliorum peccatorum, vel ipsius Adami, vel nostrorum majorum, imputatione, nullum erit malum, nec opus erit remedio. Nulla enim est causa, si D. Garissolio fides habetur, cur Deus illud peccatum nobis potius quam alia peccata, vel Adami, vel aliorum parentum, imputet, praeter unam eius voluntatem. Cum ergo id pendeat ab eius voluntate ut imputet, vel non imputet, quid opus fuit, Christum tam dira pati, ut posset nobis illud peccatum non imputari?
english: I can turn the argument on its maker. If no evil means no need of a remedy, and there is no evil unless we carry a guilt earlier than our original stain from Adam’s disobedience, and the sole true cause of that guilt in us is God’s will — then I cannot see why imputed justice is necessary at all. Let God simply withhold imputation of the first Adam’s sin, as He already withholds imputation of other sins — Adam’s own, or our forefathers’ — and there will be no evil and no need of a remedy. On Garissoles’s account there is no reason God should charge us with that sin rather than with Adam’s other sins or other parents’ sins, except His bare will. If imputing or not imputing hangs on that will alone, why did Christ have to suffer such horrors so that this sin might not be charged to us?

source_text: Possem etiam hoc loco contradictionem Domino Garissolio objicere. Ait enim, si nullus sit reatus prior corruptione, non esse opus imputata Christi justitia, & tamen alibi fatetur esse imputationem, & reatum corruptione posteriorem. Huic reatui qui corruptionem sequitur, quod justa proportione remedium respondet? sanctificatio? non opponitur proprie reatui. Justitia Christi imputata? Haec igitur, posita imputatione consequente seu mediata, nobis necessaria est. Itaque non labefactatur a Placeo doctrina de justitia Christi imputata: agnoscit enim imputationem & reatum consequentem; atque adeo peccatum originale, & satisfactionis Christi necessitatem, nihilque habet cum erroribus Socinianorum, Arminianorum &c, conjunctum.
english: I can also charge Lord Garissoles with a contradiction here. He says that if no guilt precedes corruption, we do not need Christ’s imputed justice; yet elsewhere he admits an imputation and a guilt that follow corruption. What matching remedy answers that later guilt? Sanctification? It does not properly stand against guilt. Christ’s imputed justice? Once consequent or mediate imputation is granted, that justice is what we need. So Placeus does not shake the doctrine of Christ’s imputed righteousness: he owns consequent imputation and guilt, and with them original sin and the need for Christ’s satisfaction — and he shares nothing with Socinian, Arminian, and kindred errors.

source_text: CAPUT XI. A Pelagianorum, Socinianorum, & Remonstrantium in hoc negotio sententia Placeum esse alienum. Ut nos reddat exosos, & gravissimis obruat praejudiciis, dolet nos cum Pelagianis & Socinianis paria facere. Sed dolendi causa nulla est: Nam ab hujusmodi hominum erroribus abhorremus, ut qui maxime. Vetustissimorum, addit, haereticorum (Marcionitas puto, & Manicheos, qui legem antiquam malam esse summa cum impietate afferebant) sententia fuit, nullam esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem. Quid hoc ad rem?
english: Chapter XI. That Placeus stands apart from the Pelagian, Socinian, and Remonstrant teaching on this question. Garissoles wants to make us hated and crush us under the heaviest prejudices by grieving that we make common cause with Pelagians and Socinians. There is nothing to grieve over. We shrink from the errors of such men as strongly as anyone can. He adds that the oldest heretics — I take him to mean the Marcionites and the Manichees, who with the height of impiety called the old law evil — held that there can be no just imputation of another's sin. What does that have to do with our question?

source_text: Nos-ne idem cum illis haereticis sentimus? Imo eis contradicimus. Aliquam enim esse posse justam alieni peccati imputationem credimus, & docemus; ipsiusque primi Adae peccati imputationem admittimus consequentem seu mediatam. Adde quod non in ea sententia, sed in dogmate, quod inde probare satagebant, absurdissimo eorum sita erat haeresis. Itaque quos duos testes laudat D. G. Origenem hom. 8. in Exod. & Hieronymum Comm. in Ezech. xviii. 1. 2. eos ambos laudat contra se. Cum enim Origenes protulisset illa verba, quae D. G. recitat — Videamus quomodo reddi dicantur peccata patrum in filios in tertiam & quartam generationem. In hoc enim sermone solent nos haeretici suggillare, quod non sit boni Dei sermo, qui pro peccatis alterius alterum plecti dicat — Respondet-ne, id quod D. G. respondisset, hoc minime esse injustum? Imo cum injustum id putaret, minimeque Deum decere, confugit ad sensum metaphoricum, & per parentes intelligi voluit Diabolum & angelos eius, per filios ac primam generationem eos quos Diabolus immediate seducit, per secundam eos qui ab his proxime seducuntur, per tertiam & quartam eos quos hi vel socios, vel administros peccati sibi adjungunt. Hos autem homines filios diaboli corripi & puniri in hoc saeculo, ut serventur: diabolorum vero, qui sunt eorum parentes, supplicium differri in futurum saeculum.
english: Do we agree with those heretics? On the contrary, we contradict them. We believe and teach that some just imputation of another's sin is possible, and we admit the imputation of Adam's first sin as consequent or mediate. Their heresy did not sit in that opinion, but in the absurd dogma they tried to prove from it. So the two witnesses Garissoles cites — Origen's eighth homily on Exodus, and Jerome on Ezekiel 18:1–2 — he cites against himself. When Origen had offered the words Garissoles quotes — how the fathers' sins are said to be visited on the children to the third and fourth generation, a saying heretics use to taunt us as unworthy of a good God who punishes one for another's sins — does Origen answer as Garissoles would, that this is not unjust at all? No. Thinking it unjust and unfit for God, he fled to metaphor: the 'parents' are the Devil and his angels; the first generation, those the Devil seduces directly; the second, those next seduced by them; the third and fourth, those they recruit as partners or servants of sin. Those human sons of the devil are seized and punished in this age so they may be saved; the demons who are their parents have their punishment deferred to the age to come.

source_text: Ad Hieronymum autem quod attinet, eius quidem ea sunt verba quae D. G. laudat. Sed quomodo nodum illum solvit? quomodo verba Decalogi, qui reddo peccata patrum super filios &c. interpretatur? Num ea, sicut D. G. de imputatione immediata accipit? Nullo modo. Scandalum, inquit ibidem, patiebamur occultum, quod injustitia videretur Dei, alium peccare, & alium luere peccata. Si enim reddit peccata patrum super filios in tertiam & quartam generationem, injustum videtur ut alius peccet & alius puniatur. Sed ex eo quod sequitur: His qui me oderunt, comminationis sive praecepti scandalum solvitur. Non enim ideo puniuntur in tertia & in quarta generatione, quia deliquerunt patres eorum: cum patres potius qui fuerunt peccatores, puniri debuerint: sed quia patrum extiterunt aemulatores & oderunt Deum, haereditario malo & impietate in ramos quoque de radice crescente. Quid potuit dici nostrae sententiae accommodatius? Habet idem Hieronymus paulo post haec verba. Scriptum est in Proverbiis: Sicut uva acerba dentibus noxia est: & fumus oculis: sic iniquitas his qui utuntur ea. Ex quo perspicuum est non aliorum dolere dentes & obstupescere, sed eorum qui uvam acerbam comederint. Est autem loci istius hic sensus: Quomodo si quis velit dicere: Patres uvam acerbam comederunt, & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt: ridiculum est, & nullam habens consequentiam: sic iniquum est atque perversum peccare patres, & filios nepotesque cruciari. Quid contra imputationem antecedentem dici potuit disertius?
english: As for Jerome, Garissoles does quote his words — but how does Jerome untie the knot? How does he read the Decalogue's 'I visit the fathers' sins on the children'? Does he take it, as Garissoles does, of immediate imputation? Not at all. In the same place Jerome says they were suffering a hidden scandal: it looked like God's injustice that one should sin and another pay. If God visits the fathers' sins on the children to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one sins and another is punished. But the words that follow — 'to those who hate Me' — clear the scandal. They are not punished in the third and fourth generation because their fathers sinned (the sinful fathers themselves ought to have been punished), but because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God, hereditary evil and impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. What could fit our view more closely? A little later Jerome cites Proverbs: as sour grapes hurt the teeth and smoke the eyes, so iniquity hurts those who use it — so it is plain that not other people's teeth ache, but the teeth of those who ate the sour grapes. The point of the place is: saying 'the fathers ate sour grapes and the sons' teeth went numb' is ridiculous and follows nothing; so it is unjust and twisted that fathers sin and sons and grandsons are tormented. What could be said more plainly against antecedent imputation?

source_text: His ergo missis sibi non faventibus accedit D. G. ad Pelagianos, & miratur Aegidii Hunnii ἀτοπίαν, pertendentis hanc fuisse Pelagianorum sententiam, Adami peccatum posteris imputari. Miratur etiam hallucinatum in eadem re virum doctum (Placeum designat) ita de hoc negotio in privata quadam Epistola loquentem. Qui primi immediatam (nota immediatam: hanc enim solam, minime vero mediatam, Placeus constanter improbavit) imputationem peccati Adae commenti sunt, ii Pelagiani fuerunt, qui hac ratione conati sunt anathematum adversus Pelagium vibratorum impetum declinare. Negarunt enim corruptionem haereditariam, id est, originale peccatum: & ad praestringendos Ecclesiae oculos, hoc nomine donaverunt reatum imputati primi Adae peccati. Hoc D. G. falsum esse clamat. Fatetur tamen eos qui totam rationem peccati originalis sola imputatione peccati Adae definierunt, Pelagianis accensendos esse: sed accensendos, non quia imputationem posuerint, sed quia corruptionem negaverint, &c. Id quod Aegidii Hunnii & Placei sententiam confirmat potius quam evertit. Non enim dogma de imputatione primi peccati immediata ipsi Pelagio aut omnibus Pelagianis ascripserunt: Sed illis duntaxat, qui cum essent revera Pelagiani, voluerunt non Pelagiani videri: quam ad rem inutile fuisset dogma de imputato Adae peccato, si id Pelagius aperte protulisset. Cum enim viderent, qui negarent peccatum originale pro haereticis haberi, professi sunt se peccatum originale credere: sed hoc nomine non peccatum propagatum, ut reliqui omnes orthodoxi, sed peccatum actuale Adami omnibus imputatum intelligebant. Certe illi ipsi, qui adversus Placeum imputationem immediatam urgent, imprudentes quidem, sed tamen evitare non possunt, quin Pelagianis accedant; uti jam in ipso D. Garissolio aliquoties observavi. Posito enim peccato propagato seu inhaerente, quod vere peccatum sit, ac nobis damnandis sufficiat, quid opus est alio peccato nobis imputato? posita imputatione primi Adae peccati actualis mediata, quid opus est immediata? & quomodo potest immediata ex Scriptura probari?
english: Setting aside those unhelpful witnesses, Garissoles turns to the Pelagians and marvels at Aegidius Hunnius's ἀτοπία — Hunnius's claim that the Pelagian view was that Adam's sin is imputed to posterity. He also marvels that a learned man (he means Placeus) 'hallucinated' the same way in a private letter. Those who first invented the immediate imputation of Adam's sin — note: immediate; Placeus has always rejected that alone, never the mediate — were Pelagians trying to dodge the anathemas aimed at Pelagius. They denied hereditary corruption, that is, original sin, and to dazzle the Church they gave that name to the guilt of Adam's first sin as imputed. Garissoles cries that this is false; yet he admits that anyone who makes the whole account of original sin nothing but the imputation of Adam's sin belongs with the Pelagians — not because they taught imputation, but because they denied corruption. That confirms Hunnius and Placeus more than it overturns them. They never pinned immediate imputation of the first sin on Pelagius himself or on every Pelagian, but only on those who were truly Pelagians and wanted not to look it — for if Pelagius had openly taught imputed Adam's sin, that dodge would have been useless. Seeing that deniers of original sin were counted heretics, they professed to believe original sin, but meant by it not propagated sin, as all the orthodox do, but Adam's actual sin imputed to everyone. Indeed those who press immediate imputation against Placeus cannot help sliding toward the Pelagians, as I have already noted more than once in Garissoles himself: once a propagated, inherent sin that is truly sin and enough to damn us is granted, what need is there of another sin imputed to us? Once mediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin is granted, what need of the immediate — and how can Scripture prove it?

source_text: Hic D. Garissolius multis verbis, ac prolatis aliquot testibus, confirmat Pelagium nullam imputationem Adamici peccati credidisse. Quorsum? nescio. Quis enim negat? An propterea Placeus paria facit cum Pelagio? Nonne Placei sententia Pelagianae contradicit apertissime? Pelagius omnem imputationem peccati Adae damnabat, Placeus non omnem, sed immediatam duntaxat. Ille nullam imputationem peccati Adae justam esse putabat, Placeus nonnullam esse arbitratur justam, nempe mediatam. Ille peccatum originale negabat, Placeus contra peccatum originale confitetur & probat. Qui tantopere opponuntur, quomodo paria facere dicuntur? At negat Pelagius imputationem immediatam, quam etiam Placeus negat. At, inquam, in ea negatione nunquam sita fuit haeresis Pelagiana. Non quicquid aut negavit, aut affirmavit Pelagius, continuo haereticum est. Percurramne illa omnia quae D. Garissolius Pelagianis tribuit § VI? Illi, inquit, 1. Justitiam originalem deperditam fuisse negabant. Placeus contra deperditam fuisse affirmat. Imo justitiam nullam originalem agnoscebat. Placeus justitiam originalem agnoscit. Sentiebant nos ut sine virtute sic sine vitio nasci. Sentit Placeus nos penitissime imbutos vitio nasci. Itaque infantes in illo statu esse in quo fuerat Adam ante praevaricationem. Itaque infantes non esse in eo statu in quo fuerat Adam ante praevaricationem, sed in multo deteriore. 2. Naturae humanae aliquam ab origine corruptionem inesse negabant. Placeus contra affirmat. 3. Necessitatem moriendi non habebant pro poena peccati, sed pro sequela & conditione naturae. Docebant enim Adamum sive peccasset, sive non peccasset, moriturum. Placeus habet necessitatem moriendi pro necessitate subeundi poenam, non autem pro sequela & conditione naturae. Docet enim Adamum, si non peccasset, non fuisse moriturum. 4. Poenis aeternis infantes ullos damnari negabant, eas quippe non aliunde quam ex propria uniuscujusque injustitia provenire. Placeus id non negat, quippe qui sciat poenas aeternas etiam ex innata injustitia provenire. Denique nullam omnino poenam propter Adae peccatum posteris irrogari putaverunt: Placeus contra aliquam poenam propter Adae peccatum posteris irrogari putat, nempe mortem. Itaque imputationem agnoscit immediatam peccati Adae habitualis propagati ac intra nos existentis, & mediatam peccati Adae actualis extra nos olim producti. Vides igitur, Lector, Placeum nullo modo esse Pelagianum: Quorsum ergo D. G. hoc loco patientia lectoris ad id probandum quod nemo negat, Pelagium negasse imputationem peccati Adami, abutitur, ejusque errores enumerat, quasi illorum Placeus esset particeps?
english: Here Garissoles, at length and with several witnesses, confirms that Pelagius believed in no imputation of Adam's sin. To what end? I do not know. Who denies it? Does that make Placeus Pelagius's ally? Placeus's teaching contradicts the Pelagian one as plainly as can be. Pelagius condemned every imputation of Adam's sin; Placeus condemns only the immediate. Pelagius thought no imputation of Adam's sin just; Placeus holds some just — namely the mediate. Pelagius denied original sin; Placeus confesses and proves it. How can people so opposed be said to make common cause? Yes, Pelagius denies immediate imputation, and so does Placeus — but the Pelagian heresy never sat in that denial. Not everything Pelagius denied or affirmed is heresy by that fact alone. Shall I run through all Garissoles pins on the Pelagians in section VI? (1) They denied that original justice was lost; Placeus affirms it was. Pelagius acknowledged no original justice at all; Placeus does. They held we are born without virtue and without vice; Placeus holds we are born steeped in vice. So for them infants stand where Adam stood before the fall; for Placeus infants stand in a far worse state. (2) They denied any corruption in human nature from the start; Placeus affirms it. (3) They took the necessity of dying not as sin's penalty but as nature's sequel and condition — Adam would have died whether he sinned or not; Placeus takes dying as undergoing penalty, and teaches that Adam would not have died had he not sinned. (4) They denied that any infants are damned with eternal penalties, since those come only from each one's own injustice; Placeus does not deny eternal penalties, knowing they also arise from innate injustice. Finally they thought no penalty at all is laid on posterity for Adam's sin; Placeus thinks some is — namely death. So he owns immediate imputation of Adam's habitual sin as propagated and present in us, and mediate imputation of Adam's actual sin once done outside us. Reader, Placeus is no Pelagian. Why then does Garissoles waste the reader's patience proving what no one denies — that Pelagius denied Adam's sin's imputation — and list Pelagius's errors as if Placeus shared them?

source_text: Interim quia obiter laudat ex Augustini opere imperfecto contra secundam Juliani responsionem Lutetiae edito anno hujus saeculi decimo septimo, locum, Qui, inquit, vel solus, si alius non extaret apud Augustinum, satis docet quid de hac imputatione & ipse & Ecclesia Catholica senserit, eum locum inspiciamus: Augustinus enim, si sibi constat, totus noster est. Quid est ergo quod clamas & dicis non posse Deum & dimittere peccata majoribus propter propria, & imputare parvulis aliena. (Videtur & delenda vox propter inutilis eo loco & incommoda, & sententia alio quodam mendo laborare. Non dicebat enim Julianus Deum non posse majoribus, hoc est, adultis propria dimittere peccata; sed dicebat non decere Deum, qui dimittit peccata majoribus propria, imputare parvulis aliena.) Nec vis attendere quod nonnisi in Christo renatis, utraque; non renatis autem in Christo neutra dimittantur. Ipsa sunt enim Christiana & gratiae sacramenta abscondita sapientibus & prudentibus & revelata parvulis. In quibus, o si esses, nec quasi magnus in tua virtute consideres, profecto intelligeres, sic imputari generatis parvulis injustitiam primi hominis ad subeundum supplicium, quemadmodum imputatur parvulis regeneratis justitia secundi hominis ad obtinendum regnum coelorum. Nobis hic locus minime nocet. Imputationem enim intelligit, quae generationem, atque adeo ingenitam corruptionem sequitur; cum imputatio, quam negamus, ut corruptionem sic generationem antecedere putetur; causa enim creditur esse, cur gignamur corrupti. Adde quod nihil prohibet per injustitiam primi hominis, injustitiam intelligere habitualem, quam ad parvulos primus homo per generationem transmisit. Certe enim cum Augustino objiceretur a Pelagianis, Qui fieri possit, ut Deus, qui pro sua bonitate nostra ipsorum peccata remittit, velit imputare aliena? Respondit, teste Martyre, Deum summe bonum esse, neque, quod isti assumunt, in culpa originis imputare nobis alienum peccatum, sed nostram ipsorum iniquitatem, quae nostrae naturae adhaeret jam inde ab ipsa origine. Addam aliud ejusdem Martyris de Augustino testimonium. Augustinus, inquit, in Enchiridio ad Laurentium capite 46. probabile ait esse, peccata etiam proximorum parentum communicari cum filiis. Ad quod probandum componit inter se duo loca Scripturarum a nobis ante tractata: Quod Deus ait, se velle persequi peccata patrum in filios in tertiam, & quartam generationem: quum alio loco dicat, Filium non portaturum iniquitatem patris. Si filius, inquit, non portat iniquitatem patris, sed suam, & tamen Deus persequitur in eo peccatum patris, oportet, ut filius ipse peccatum illud in se habeat: Alioqui haec loca inter se non convenirent. Num haec dixisset Augustinus, si peccati paterni imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam credidisset, qua scilicet filius sit peccator & reus, alioqui non peccator, nec reus?
english: Meanwhile Garissoles casually praises a passage from Augustine's unfinished work against Julian's second reply (Paris, in the seventeenth year of this century) — a passage which, he says, even alone would show what Augustine and the Catholic Church thought about this imputation. Let us look at it: if Augustine is consistent, he is wholly ours. What then is this cry — that God cannot both forgive adults their own sins and impute another's to little ones? (The word propter also looks deletable there as useless and awkward, and the sentence has some other fault. Julian was not saying God cannot forgive adults their own sins; he was saying it does not become the God who forgives adults their own to impute another's to little ones.) Nor will you face this: only those reborn in Christ have both forgiven; those not reborn in Christ have neither. The Christian sacraments of grace are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones. If you were among them, and did not think yourself great in your own virtue, you would see that the first man's injustice is imputed to little ones as generated, for undergoing punishment, just as the second man's justice is imputed to little ones as regenerated, for obtaining the kingdom of heaven. That place does not hurt us. Augustine means an imputation that follows generation — and so inborn corruption — whereas the imputation we deny is supposed to precede generation as it does corruption, as if it were the cause of our being born corrupt. Nothing stops us taking 'the first man's injustice' as habitual injustice transmitted to little ones by generation. When the Pelagians asked Augustine how God, who in His goodness remits our own sins, could will to impute another's, he answered (Martyr witnesses) that God is supremely good and does not, as they assume, impute another's sin to us in the guilt of origin, but our own iniquity, which already clings to our nature from the origin itself. Martyr adds another witness: in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 46, Augustine says it is probable that even the nearest parents' sins are shared with the children. To prove it he sets together two Scriptures we already treated: God will pursue the fathers' sins on the children to the third and fourth generation, yet elsewhere the son shall not bear the father's iniquity. If the son does not bear the father's iniquity but his own, and yet God pursues the father's sin in him, the son must have that sin in himself — otherwise the places would not agree. Would Augustine have said that if he had believed an antecedent or immediate imputation of the father's sin, by which a son would be sinner and guilty who otherwise would be neither?

source_text: De Socinianis, cum nihil differant a Pelagianis, quid opus est dicere? Ad Arminianos autem quod spectat, ab eorum etiam erroribus, Dei beneficio, abhorret Placeus. Qui autem pro Clariss. Molineo Respondit Corvino doctissimus Walaeus, is non dubitavit imputationem immediatam disertis verbis negare, uti a nobis observatum est supra, pag. 22. nec propterea partibus Remonstrantium favere existimatur. Atque haec fuerunt argumenta D. Garissolii.
english: As for the Socinians, since they differ not at all from the Pelagians, what more is there to say? As for the Arminians, by God's kindness Placeus shrinks from their errors too. The learned Walaeus, answering Corvinus for the distinguished Du Moulin, did not hesitate to deny immediate imputation in plain words — as we noted above at page 22 — and is not for that reason thought to side with the Remonstrants. And those were Lord Garissoles's arguments.

source_text: CAPUT XII. Imputationem antecedentem seu immediatam non esse probatam argumentis Dom. Daubuz. Nam cum libro D. Garissolii prodit ad eum Epistola & carmen propempticum Caroli Daubuz V.D. in Ecclesia Neracensi Ministri, quibus vehementer eum laudat, & in Placeum invehitur. Affert autem pro imputatione peccati Adamici argumenta eadem, sed verbis paulo diversis. Orditur autem a foedere inito cum Adamo, idque supponit non probat: Aitque nos cum Adamo fuisse; et ut cum eo, ac per eum agentes et consentientes, pari poena plectendos. At, amabo te, quomodo cum Adamo fuimus, qui tunc nulli fuimus? Prius enim est nos esse, quam esse cum alio. Quomodo cum eo egimus? Non enim agit nisi qui est, & quidem persona vel suppositum: actiones enim sunt suppositorum. Quomodo cum eo & per eum consensimus? Est enim consensio nostra voluntatis nostrae, quatenus ab Adamo differimus, actio. Quod si hanc consensionem nihil aliud vult esse quam corruptionem haereditariam nobis ingenitam, ex ea nihil conficietur praeter imputationem mediatam, quam Placeus probat. Addit pro ratione, Quandoquidem ex Iurisconsultorum placitis, qui per alium facit, per se ipsum facere videtur. At, inquam, id erat non supponendum sed probandum, Nos per Adamum id fecisse, quod fecit Adamus. Auscultavitne voci uxoris suae loco nostro? nosne illi fuimus autores ut peccaret? aut peccavitne ut minister noster, nos ut causae principales?
english: Chapter XII. That Lord Daubuz's arguments do not prove antecedent or immediate imputation. With Garissoles's book there also appeared a letter and a farewell poem from Charles Daubuz, minister of the Word in the church at Nerac — warm praise for Garissoles, and an attack on Placeus. He urges the same case for imputing Adam's sin, only in slightly different words. He opens from a covenant made with Adam, and he takes that as given rather than proving it. We were with Adam, he says; and as agents and consenters with him and through him we deserve the same penalty. But how, I ask, were we with Adam when we did not yet exist? Existing comes before existing-with-another. How did we act with him? Only what exists acts, and that as a person or subject — for actions belong to subjects. How did we consent with him and through him? Our consent is an act of our own will precisely as we differ from Adam. If by 'consent' he means nothing but the hereditary corruption born in us, he gets only mediate imputation — which Placeus already grants. He adds the lawyers' maxim: whoever acts through another seems to act through himself. That, I say, was not to be assumed but proved: that through Adam we did what Adam did. Did Adam heed his wife in our place? Were we the authors of her sin? Or did he sin as our servant while we were the principal causes?

source_text: Sed his missis argumentatur ex Scriptura, & primo ex verbis ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. Peccavimus, inquit, in Adamo, Ergo illius peccati participes, rei; ergo imputabile iure, & imputatum delictum illud. Primum esto, imputetur, modo id fieri intelligatur mediante corruptione, quid hoc contra nos? Deinde, nego verba ἐφ᾽ ᾧ verti debere in quo. Id probare conatur autoritate eorum qui sic verterunt, quibus nominatis concludit, Hinc patere, quam praecipitanter, aut quam oscitanter non nemo scripserit, nec τὸ ἐφ᾽ ᾧ verti debere in quo, sed eo quod. Quae accusatio una cum Placeo eos omnes petit, qui maluerunt eo quod, vel quatenus, vel quoniam, &c. quam in quo, vertere: qui haud dubie, si putassent verti debere in quo, versionem illam retinuissent; si non putassent verti debere eo quod &c., non eo quod vertissent. Caeterum & nobis respondentibus satis est posse verti eo quod &c., & sic debere reddi probatum est supra pag. 70. & seqq. Denique, ut dicamur peccasse in Adamo satis est, si peccatum Adami causa fuerit peccati nostri, sicut eius esse nostri esse causa fuit.
english: Leaving that aside, he turns to Scripture, and first to ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον. We sinned in Adam, he says; therefore we share his sin and stand guilty; therefore the offense is rightly imputable — and imputed. Grant the imputation, so long as it comes by way of corruption: what does that do against us? Next I deny that ἐφ᾽ ᾧ must mean 'in whom.' He leans on translators who so rendered it, names them, and concludes that someone has written rashly or sleepily who said τὸ ἐφ᾽ ᾧ should not be 'in whom' but 'because.' That charge hits Placeus and everyone who preferred 'because,' 'inasmuch as,' 'since,' and the like to 'in whom.' Had they thought 'in whom' required, they would have kept it; had they not thought 'because' right, they would not have written 'because.' For our answer it is enough that 'because' is possible — and that it is the right rendering was already shown above at page 70 and following. Finally, to say we sinned in Adam it is enough that Adam's sin caused ours, just as his being caused ours.

source_text: Demus tamen, inquit Vir doctus, illud gratis, an eius loci vim penitus infringunt? Nequaquam certe: nam illud τὸ peccarunt in infantibus verissimum, peccatum quoddam actuale designat evidenter. Hoc nego, negaruntque ante me plurimi viri maximi, inter quos Calvinus & Martyr: ac, si me decet recriminari, de peccato actuali illud peccarunt exponebant Pelagiani. At quod quaeso peccatum peccaverit infans in matris utero latens, in cunis vagiens? Peccavit certe non actu sed habitu, non peccatum actuale sed originale. Originale quidem, inquit, habet, sed καθ᾽ ἕξιν potius subjective, quam ἐνεργείᾳ. Nimirum non est actio sed qualitas potius: sese enim habet ad modum habitus. An propterea minus vere peccatum est, nos reatu, nisi condonetur, obstringens? Ergo, addit, quod morimur a teneris annis, ab ipsis unguiculis: imo quod vix nati denascimur, ideo fit (fatemur) quia peccavimus; at peccare nisi in Adamo tunc non potuimus. Quid est negare vitium originale esse vere peccatum toti generi humano damnando (ut habet art. XI. Confessionis Fidei) sufficiens, si hoc non est? Causam profecto Pighii vir hic doctus agit imprudens. Quid enim? Annon ab ipso utero materno peccatores in nobis ipsis sumus? inhaerente peccato involuti ac contaminati?
english: Grant them that for free, says the learned man: do they still gut the force of the text? Not at all. That 'they sinned' said of infants is most true, he claims, and plainly marks some actual sin. I deny it — and many great men before me did, Calvin and Martyr among them. If I may turn the charge, it was the Pelagians who took that 'they sinned' of an actual sin. What sin has an infant committed while still in the womb, or crying in the cradle? He has sinned not by act but by habit — not actual sin but original. Original, Daubuz says, he does have, but καθ᾽ ἕξιν, subjectively, rather than ἐνεργείᾳ. In other words it is not an action but a quality, standing as a habit stands. Is it therefore less truly a sin, binding us in guilt unless forgiven? So, he adds, we die from tender years, from the fingertips; indeed we scarcely born die again — because, we confess, we have sinned; yet then we could sin only in Adam. What is denying that original vice is truly a sin enough to damn the whole race (as Article XI of the Confession says), if this is not that denial? Without noticing it, this learned man is pleading Pighius's cause. Are we not sinners in ourselves from the maternal womb — wrapped and stained in inherent sin?

source_text: incredulitate, malitia, &c. penitus imbuti, ac propterea iustificationis & regenerationis gratia egentes? Si fateris, quomodo negas nos peccasse, nos esse peccatores in nobis ipsis? Si negas, iisdem tecum argumentis agere necesse erit, quibus olim adversus Pelagium, & superiore saeculo adversus Pighium disputatum est. Quod tamen subiungit, Illam mortem culpam actualem mediate saltem praesupponere, ambiguum est. Si culpam actualem habituali opponit, quid inde sequi potest, nisi culpam actualem Adami mediate nobis imputari? id quod damus libenter. Sin culpam actualem opponit potentiali, etiam peccatum originale culpa actualis dici potest: est enim in nobis non potestate sed actu, eiusque reatus eo sensu non minus actualis dici potest quam reatus peccati actualis. Affirmanti igitur D. Daubuz, nec probanti oppono Theodoretum, Ad omnes homines mors pervasit, quatenus omnes peccaverunt: Non enim propter primi parentis peccatum: sed propter suum unusquisque mortis decretum contraxit. Oppono etiam Augustinum, Propter hoc ergo solum vitium, sicut in eo libro cui resistis, a me scriptum est, humana natura damnatur, & propter quod damnatur, damnabili diabolo subiugatur, quia & ipse diabolus spiritus immundus est. Ut tam debili argumento colorem aliquem conciliet obviam it cuidam responsioni Placei. In eo, inquit, quod addunt illi, quibus ab adversis partibus hic stare placuit, & fallendo falluntur, ne hilum quidem proficiunt. Non est, inquiunt, cur in Adamo, aliter peccasse, quam fuisse aut mori dicamur. O nodum ἀδιάλυτον!
english: Thoroughly soaked in unbelief, malice, and the rest — and therefore needing the grace of justification and regeneration? If you grant that, how do you deny that we have sinned, that we are sinners in ourselves? If you deny it, one must meet you with the same weapons once used against Pelagius, and in the last age against Pighius. His further claim — that that death at least mediately presupposes an actual fault — is ambiguous. If 'actual' is set against 'habitual,' what follows except that Adam's actual fault is mediately imputed to us? We gladly grant that. If 'actual' is set against 'potential,' even original sin can be called an actual fault: it is in us in act, not in potency, and its guilt in that sense is no less actual than the guilt of an actual sin. So to Daubuz affirming without proving I oppose Theodoret: Death has spread to all inasmuch as all have sinned — not for the first parent's sin, but each has drawn the sentence of death for his own. I also oppose Augustine: For this one vice alone, as I wrote in the book you resist, human nature is condemned, and for that for which it is condemned it is subjected to the damnable devil, for the devil himself is an unclean spirit. To paint so weak an argument he meets a reply of Placeus. Those who take the other side, he says, add something and by deceiving are deceived — and gain nothing. There is no reason, they say, to speak of sinning in Adam otherwise than of being or dying in him. O insoluble knot (ἀδιάλυτον)!

source_text: Atqui in Adamo fuimus dupliciter ἁπλῶς & κατὰ μέρος, scilicet repraesentative & naturaliter; tota quidem natura humana, quae citra dubium fuit in Adamo (ut ait Thom. in cap. 5. ad Rom. Lect. 3. circa finem; Nos fuimus in Adamo secundum corpulentam substantiam & secundum seminalem rationem) & per personam peccavit in Adamo, rea fuit & culpae tunc commissae & poenae futurae. Primum non argumentatur Placeus, sed respondet. Est-ne igitur illud quod respondet verum, an falsum? Si verum, non fallendo falluntur. Si falsum, falsitas ostendenda fuit. Id quod a viro docto non fit. Latebat autem in responsione illa Placei duplex argumentum, unum ab existentia, alterum a morte. Illud sic potest concipi; Non aliter in Adamo peccasse quam fuisse dicimur. Atqui in Adamo non dicimur fuisse imputative; eius enim esse nobis non imputatur: sed tantum eius esse in nos est propagatum. Ergo nec peccasse dicendi sumus in Adamo imputative, sed reali peccati eius per propagationem naturalem communicatione. Item sic; Non aliter in Adamo peccavimus quam fuimus. Atqui non fuimus in Adamo proxime seu immediate, sed mediantibus parentibus nostris intermediis ab eo propagatis. Ergo non peccavimus in Adamo proxime seu immediate, sed mediantibus parentum nostrorum ab eo propagatis originalibus vitiis. Argumentum vero ductum a morte, sic potest formari. Non aliter in Adamo peccavisse quam mori dicimur. Sed morimur in Adamo, non imputata nobis Adami morte, sed morte reapse in nos propagata. Ergo peccavimus in Adamo, non imputato eius peccato, sed peccato reapse in nos propagato. Probat-ne, aut respondet aliquid Vir doctus, quod hujusmodi argumenta destruat, aut aliquomodo infirmet? Nihil prorsus.
english: Yet we were in Adam two ways, Daubuz says — ἁπλῶς and κατὰ μέρος, representatively and naturally. Whole human nature was in Adam without doubt (so Thomas on Romans 5, lecture 3 near the end: we were in Adam by bodily substance and by seminal reason); and in Adam the person sinned, so nature was guilty of the fault then done and of the punishment to come. First: Placeus is not arguing here but answering. Is that answer true or false? If true, they are not 'deceived by deceiving.' If false, the falsehood should have been shown. The learned man does not show it. Inside Placeus's reply there lay a double argument — one from existence, one from death. From existence: we are not said to have sinned in Adam otherwise than to have been in him. But we are not said to have been in him by imputation; his being is not imputed to us — it is only propagated into us. Therefore we are not to be said to have sinned in him by imputation either, but by a real sharing of his sin through natural propagation. Again: we did not sin in Adam otherwise than we were in him. But we were not in him immediately, only through intermediate parents descended from him. Therefore we did not sin in him immediately, only through our parents' original vices descended from him. From death: we are not said to have sinned in Adam otherwise than to die in him. But we die in him not because his death is imputed, but because death is actually propagated into us. Therefore we sinned in him not by imputed sin, but by sin actually propagated into us. Does the learned man prove or answer anything that breaks or even weakens arguments of this kind? Nothing at all.

source_text: Negat-ne an fatetur, nos non aliter in Adamo peccasse quam fuisse? Tantum ait nos fuisse in Adamo dupliciter, repraesentative & naturaliter. Aitne ergo, an negat esse Adami nobis imputari? Saltem explicasset quid sibi voluit illa distinctione; & an similiter peccaverimus in Adamo repraesentative & naturaliter, ac itidem in eo dupliciter mortui simus? Probatne igitur duplicem illum modum? Nequaquam. Tantum Reformatus apud Reformatum agens pro testimonio Scripturae, pro ratione, Thomam Aquinatem laudat dicentem, Nos fuisse in Adamo secundum corpulentam substantiam & secundum seminalem rationem. Hoccine est esse in Adamo dupliciter, repraesentative scilicet & naturaliter? Et, an similiter peccavimus in Adamo? Illustrat tamen hoc similitudine, Et si quondam vere dixit ille, in uno Caesare plures inesse Marios, quam verius nobis dicere licet, in uno Adamo peccante plures, imo omnes (excepto Christo θεανθρώπῳ) fuisse Adamos. Quid potuit afferri minus appositum? Num inde potuit colligi, aliquam Caesaris actionem pluribus Mariis imputandam fuisse? Num fuerunt plures Marii repraesentative & naturaliter, vel secundum corpulentam substantiam & seminalem rationem, in Caesare? Non miseret te mei, Lector prudentissime, cui cum talibus disputatoribus tanti momenti negotium est? Porro, inquit, adeant illi Docti viri, qui nonnisi nimia subtilitatis & scientiae opinione nunc errant. Erremusne, necne, tuum esto, quisquis haec legis, iudicium. Nobisne insit nimia subtilitatis & scientiae opinio, is novit qui corda scrutatur: Nos certe, quantum possumus, abiecta eiusmodi opinione, ab eo uno pendemus. Sed pergat, Adeant, inquam, consulant tribunalia iudicum, subsellia Iurisconsultorum. Annon actores publici, legati, tabelliones, & eiusmodi homines, qui pro aliis stant, eos etiam absentes referant, ceu praesentes sistant, repraesentent, ut hoc, etsi ambiguo, nuncupar verbo? Et quanto magis in hoc foedere: optimates, pater, stirps, caput, auctor totius generis humani, posteros omnes in publico & communi pacto repraesentaverit? Egregia consequentia! scilicet Adamus erat legatus noster, aut tabellio noster! Erat saltem pater, stirps, caput nostrum, nimirum postquam nos genuit: antequam enim inciperet gignere profecto pater non fuit. Docet ergo nos potius adire oracula divina clamantia, neque patrem filii, neque filium patris iniquitatem laturum.
english: Does he deny or admit that we did not sin in Adam otherwise than we were? He only says we were in Adam two ways — representatively and naturally. Does he then affirm or deny that Adam's being is imputed to us? He should at least have explained that distinction — and whether we likewise sinned in Adam both ways, and died in him both ways. Does he prove the double mode? Not at all. A Reformed man speaking to a Reformed man, instead of Scripture or a reason, he cites Thomas: we were in Adam by bodily substance and by seminal reason. Is that 'being in Adam doubly' — representatively and naturally? And did we likewise sin in him? He dresses it with a likeness: if someone once truly said many Mariuses are in one Caesar, how much more truly may we say that in one sinning Adam there were many Adams — indeed all, except Christ the God-man (θεάνθρωπος). What could be less to the point? Does it follow that some act of Caesar is to be imputed to many Mariuses? Were many Mariuses in Caesar representatively and naturally, or by bodily substance and seminal reason? Do you not pity me, prudent reader, stuck in business of this weight with such disputants? Further, he says, let those learned men go who now err only by too high an opinion of their own subtlety and knowledge. Whether we err, let the reader judge. Whether that opinion is in us, he knows who searches hearts; as far as we can we cast it off and hang on him alone. But let him continue: let them consult the judges' tribunals and the lawyers' benches. Do not public actors, ambassadors, notaries, and such who stand for others also report the absent, set them as present, represent them — if I may use that ambiguous word? And how much more in this covenant would the chiefs, father, stock, head, and author of the whole race have represented all posterity in a public common pact? Fine consequence! So Adam was our ambassador — or our notary! He was at least our father, stock, and head — namely after he begot us; before he began to beget he was certainly no father. Better to go to the divine oracles that cry: the father shall not bear the son's iniquity, nor the son the father's.

source_text: Ad foedus quod spectat, qualenam intelligit? Gratiae? Legale? Non arbitror. Naturae? Id quale intelligitur velim mihi exponi. Video enim duplicem latam fuisse Adamo legem: Unam per signa naturaliter significantia, Alteram per signa ex instituto significantia; illam naturae insitam, hanc verbo revelatam. Sub illa fuit Adamus, quatenus homo ac mundi incola; sub hac vero, quatenus incola paradisi. Utra foedus illud fuit? Non ista, ut opinor. His enim verbis concepta fuit, De omni arbore horti comedendo comedes. De arbore vero scientiae boni & mali non comedes ex ea: Nam quocunque die comederis ex ea moriendo morieris. Quae lex nec foederis prae se fert naturam, & tunc lata est Adamo, cum defectu uxoris (quae supernaturaliter creanda erat) pater esse non posset. Dices illam legem toti generi humano latam fuisse. Omnino lata fuit toti generi humano quod tunc extabat: at non ei, quod neque erat, neque paradisi unquam incola fuit. Fuerit tamen lata toti generi humano, num illius prima violatio actualis profecta ab uno homine, omnibus illius hominis posteris, a quibus violata non est, imputari debuit? Nonne lex Mosaica toti populo Israelitico lata fuit? Et tamen prima illius legis violatio non est omnibus posteris eorum, quibus primum lata est, imputata. Nonne foedus divinitus cum Abrahamo percussum fuit? Idque pro se & semine suo Abrahamus accepit? Numergo Abrahami actio vel una, vel plures, omnibus eius posteris imputatur? Estne quicquam in illa lege, unde eiusmodi imputatio elici possit? Non est ergo lex illa tale foedus, quod talem imputationem importet. Sed neque etiam huiusmodi foedus est lex seu foedus quod vulgo natura appellatur. Sub ea quidem nascuntur omnes homines: Sed in ea nihil potest deprehendi, unde primi Adae peccati actualis antecedens seu immediata imputatio colligi possit. Non magis enim pertinent ad omnes homines eius comminationes quam mandata: Nec minus tenentur posteri Adami pro se quisque eam observare, quam tenebatur olim Adamus. Sed fortasse diutius, quam par est, in nudis assertionibus, ac, ut loquuntur, principii petitionibus refellendis immoror.
english: As for the covenant — which kind does he mean? Of grace? Legal? I think not. Of nature? Let him tell me what that is supposed to be. I see a double law laid on Adam: one through signs that signify by nature, one through signs that signify by institution — the first planted in nature, the second revealed by the word. Under the first Adam stood as man and world-dweller; under the second, as paradise-dweller. Which was 'that covenant'? Not the second, I think. It was framed in these words: Of every tree of the garden you may freely eat; but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day you eat of it you shall surely die. That law does not wear a covenant's face, and it was laid on Adam when, for want of a wife still to be created supernaturally, he could not be a father. You will say it was laid on the whole human race. It was laid on the whole race that then existed — not on a race that did not yet exist and never dwelt in paradise. Grant it was laid on the whole race: must its first actual breach by one man be imputed to all his posterity who did not break it? Was not the Mosaic law laid on all Israel? Yet its first breach is not imputed to all the posterity of those who first received it. Was not a covenant struck with Abraham for himself and his seed? Are one or more of Abraham's acts therefore imputed to all his posterity? Is there anything in that law from which such an imputation can be drawn? So that law is not a covenant that imports such an imputation. Nor is the law or covenant commonly called nature such a covenant. All men are born under it; but nothing in it yields an antecedent or immediate imputation of Adam's first actual sin. Its threats belong to all men no more than its commands; and Adam's posterity are each as bound to keep it for themselves as Adam once was. But perhaps I linger too long refuting bare assertions and, as they say, beggings of the question.

source_text: Tranfit ille Vir doctus ad vers. XIX. Ex eoque sic argumentatur. Constituti sumus peccatores per inobedientiam Adami; Ergo nobis imputata fuit. Mediante corruptione hereditaria, Concedo: Immediate, Nego. Videtur probare velle consequentiam. Nam qui quaeso, inquit, illa κατάστασις, illa ἁμαρτία, illud παράπτωμα, nos potuit reos constituere, τὸ παράπτωμα Rom. vers. 18. (quod quidem est actus judiciarius, justitiae Dei effatum, & effectum, damnatio, condemnatio) in nos inducere citra peccatum actuale, vel proprium, vel imputatum? Apage hoc delirium. Facilis est responsio. Potest nos reos constituere, ut loquitur Chamierus, causaliter, producto & propagato in nos peccato originali. Neque id est delirium; sed constans Ecclesiae doctrina, quam veram esse Scriptura & experientia contestantur. Quomodo, subjungit, constitui peccatores, scilicet actu, sine peccato? Quod cum non possit esse originale, quippe quod tantum adhuc habituale, praesertim in recens conceptis aut natis, superest ut sit quoddam actuale peccatum. Respondeo, constitui peccatores non sine peccato: nam peccatum originale est vere peccatum. At non est actu. Imo est actu peccatum habituale: actu inhaeret infantibus: actu nos facit reos irae divinae. Hoc si negas, a Pighii opinione vix distas.
english: That learned man moves on to verse 19, and argues from it: we were made sinners by Adam's disobedience, therefore it was imputed to us. Through hereditary corruption—I grant; immediately—I deny. He seems bent on proving the consequence. Who, he asks, could that κατάστασις, that ἁμαρτία, that παράπτωμα make us guilty, or bring the παράπτωμα of Romans 5:18 (a judicial act, God's justice spoken out, and its effect: damnation, condemnation) upon us without actual sin, whether our own or imputed? Away with the delirium. The answer is plain. As Chamier puts it, it can make us guilty causally, by original sin produced and propagated into us. That is no delirium; it is the Church's settled doctrine, which Scripture and experience confirm. How, he adds, can we be constituted sinners in act without sin? Since that cannot be original sin—still only habitual, especially in the newly conceived or newborn—it must be some actual sin. I answer: we are constituted sinners not without sin, for original sin is truly sin. It is not an actual act; it is, in act, habitual sin: in act it inheres in infants; in act it makes us liable to God's wrath. Deny that, and you are scarcely off Pighius's path.

source_text: Suggillat etiam nostram responsionem, In re sitam esse similitudinem oppositionis, non in rei modo; ac dicit nos Socini potius quam Calvini partes tueri: cum tamen ipse revera discedat a Calvino, cui nos arcte adhaeremus. Quomodo autem illam responsionem, quam supra & autoritate & ratione comprobavimus, refutat? petit, cur ergo nostrates justificationis nostrae modum, nempe per imputationem justitiae Christi hinc eliciunt? Haec est scilicet egregia refutandi ratio! Quinam vero sunt illi nostrates qui id hinc eliciunt? Calvinus? Martyr? Bucerus? Bullingerus &c? Nequaquam certe; sed recentiores, ab eorum vestigiis ea in re deflectentes. At, inquit, non vident quantum communem causam laedant, qui hoc sibi invictum argumentum non solum eripi patiuntur, sed & nobis, ut adversae causae faveant, quantum in eis situm est, eripiunt. Et si cur hunc locum ita luxent, anquiramus; id in gratiam Pelagianorum, Arminianorum, Socinianorum, Anabaptistarum fieri certo comperiemus. Imo vero videmus quantum causam communem laedant, qui bene argumentari, vel nesciunt vel nolunt, argumentaque nullius roboris pro invictis obtrudunt, & interim fratres suos calumniis obruunt. Hoc certe & videmus & dolemus.
english: He also gibes at our reply—that the opposition's likeness lies in the thing, not in its mode—and says we take Socinus's part rather than Calvin's, when in fact he is the one leaving Calvin, to whom we hold fast. How does he refute the reply we already proved by authority and reason? He asks why our people then draw from this text the mode of justification, namely by imputing Christ's righteousness. A fine refutation! Who among ours draws that from here—Calvin, Martyr, Bucer, Bullinger, and the rest? Not at all; only later writers who leave their path on this point. They do not see, he says, how they wound the common cause when they let this supposedly invincible argument be torn from them—and, so far as they can, tear it from us to favor the other side. If we ask why they luxuriate so in this place, we shall find it is done to favor Pelagians, Arminians, Socinians, and Anabaptists. We see the opposite: they wound the common cause who cannot or will not argue well, push forward weak proofs as invincible, and meanwhile bury their brothers under slander. That we both see and lament.

source_text: Caetera praetermitto, nudas sine ratione affirmationes: illud tantum subiungam, quod & speciem aliquam prae se fert argumenti, & quam a publica fidei nostrae Confessione recedant & ad Pighianismum accedant illi qui nos accusant, prodit. Si peccatum, inquit, primi parentis non imputatur, quid opus imputatione meritorum Christi? Si vel peccatum originale intelligeret, vel imputationem mediatam, nihil diceret causae, quam agimus repugnans, diceret tantum aliquid falsum, & Theologo indignum, ne dicam Christiano. Opus enim nobis est imputatione justitiae Christi, ut etiam ab aliis peccatis nostris, quae nimium multa sunt, justificemur: Sed cum peccatum actuale Adami intelligat, illiusque imputationem immediatam, quis non videt ab eo peccati originalis reatum negari? Idque peccatum, quantum ad condemnationem vel justificationem attinet, pro nullo haberi? Sufficit, addit, sanctificatio quae tollat illum morbum. Est-ne igitur, inquam, ita morbus ut non sit peccatum? ut non damnet? Confer quaeso cum hujusmodi hominum doctrina articulum XI. Confessionis fidei; Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes & singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet, quamvis qui filii Dei sunt, minime idcirco condemnentur, quoniam videlicet Deus pro gratuita sua bonitate & misericordia illud ipsis non imputat. Dicimus praeterea hanc perversitatem semper edere fructus aliquos malitiae & rebellionis, &c.
english: I leave the rest—bare assertions without reason—and add only this, which both looks like an argument and shows how far our accusers leave our public Confession and drift toward Pighianism. If, he says, the first parent's sin is not imputed, why impute Christ's merits? Had he meant original sin or mediate imputation, he would not contradict our cause; he would only say something false and unfit for a theologian, let alone a Christian. We need Christ's righteousness imputed so we may also be justified from our many other sins. But when he means Adam's actual sin and its immediate imputation, who does not see that he denies original sin's guilt, and treats that sin as nothing for condemnation or justification? Sanctification that removes the disease is enough, he adds. Is it then a disease that is not sin, that does not condemn? Set that teaching beside Confession article XI: we believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every human being—even infants still in the womb—liable to eternal death before God. We also affirm that even after baptism it remains truly sin as to blame, though the sons of God are not therefore condemned, because God of free goodness and mercy does not impute it to them. We add that this perversity always bears some fruits of malice and rebellion.

source_text: Vides hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, omnes homines aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragere, nisi condonetur, imputari, & negabis nobis opus esse imputatione meritorum Christi ut justificemur ab hoc vitio? Ita qui nobis in hac causa adversantur ejus culpae rei sunt, cujus nos falso accusant: discedunt enim a recepta doctrina. Quod ergo addit, O sic tota illa nostrae justificationis evangelicae doctrina, quam eximia, quam admiranda! ex horum φρονημάτων aut corruet tota, aut saltem inutilis reddetur; cernis, ut opinor, Lector, quam falsum & calumniosum sit. Idem accidit Clarissimo viro D. Steph. Blanco, cujus Disputatio Theologica de animae humanae origine, & modo quo propagatur peccatum originale prodiit in lucem eodem anno 1648. Is enim Th. XLII. sic disputat. Omnes peccaverunt peccato scilicet illo, quod per unum hominem introiit in mundum; at non peccaverunt peccato illo in sua persona, quia non extiterunt. Ergo peccaverunt in Adamo, quippe in quo mortui sunt I. Cor. 15. 22. Quanquam enim admitti posset conclusio, si recte intelligeretur; tamen minor propositio nihil aliud esse videtur, quam eius negatio, quod articulo illo XI. ab Ecclesiis nostris asseritur. Negat enim vitium illud esse peccatum quod per unum hominem in mundum, id est, in omnes homines introiit, quod tamen vitium in illo articulo & vere peccatum esse, & omnes & singulos homines reos mortis aeternae coram Deo peragere dicitur; quod efficere non posset, nisi in omnes & singulos homines introiisset.
english: You see this vice is truly sin, that it makes every man liable to eternal death before God unless it is forgiven—that it is imputed—and will you still deny we need Christ's merits imputed to be justified from it? So our opponents in this cause are guilty of the very charge they falsely lay on us: they leave the received doctrine. When he adds how excellent and wonderful our whole evangelical justification would look—yet from these φρονημάτα it must either fall wholly or at least become useless—you see, Reader, how false and slanderous that is.
